Routers forward packets between different IP networks, which is what separate VLANs represent. A Layer 2 switch alone forwards only within a VLAN, so learning more MAC addresses does not solve inter-VLAN routing.
options: A firewall, to encrypt traffic between the VLANs
An access point, to broadcast both SSIDs to all hosts
A switch, to learn the MAC addresses in both VLANs
A router or Layer 3 device, to forward packets between different IP networks
q: A branch office has two VLANs that cannot exchange traffic even though hosts reach other devices in their own VLAN. Which device role must be added or configured to forward traffic between the VLANs?

explain: A switch forwards frames selectively using its MAC address table, so unrelated ports do not receive the traffic. A router forwards between networks, not between hosts that are already on the same local network in this scenario.
options: Name resolution, by mapping hostnames to IP addresses
Routing, by choosing the best path to a remote network
Switching, by forwarding frames only to the destination MAC address port
Firewalling, by inspecting traffic against access rules
q: A user reports that four PCs plugged into the same office device can exchange files at full speed after the device learns their addresses, without traffic reaching a fifth PC. Which role is the device performing?

explain: A firewall enforces security policy by permitting or denying traffic between zones, such as inside and outside. A controller manages network devices and does not itself filter user traffic at the boundary in this way.
options: Server
Firewall
Endpoint
Controller
q: An engineer places a device between the LAN and the internet that permits outbound web traffic from inside hosts but blocks unsolicited inbound connection attempts. Which role is being described?

explain: Endpoints are user devices that originate or consume services, while servers provide services or data to many clients. Reversing them ignores who is requesting and who is providing the resource.
options: The workstation is a server and the central system is an endpoint
The workstation is an endpoint and the central system is a server
Both are firewalls because both process requests
Both are controllers

Two-tier architecture

explain: Mode active = LACP initiates negotiation. Both sides' parameters (speed, duplex, VLAN) must

q: Which are the three planes of network operation?
options: Core, distribution, access
LAN, WAN, WLAN
Physical, virtual, cloud
Management, control, data
explain: Management (admin), control (routing intelligence), data (packet forwarding).

q: Two switches contend to be root: A runs priority 32768 with MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:01; B runs priority 32768 with MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:02. Which switch wins the election?
options: The switch with the highest IP address
The switch with the most ports
The switch that booted first, always
Switch A — bridge ID priority 32768, MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:01
explain: The lowest bridge ID wins — priority first, then lowest MAC as tiebreaker. Switch A has the lower bridge ID (priority 32768, MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:01).

q: Switch A has priority 4096 and MAC 00:aa:bb:cc:dd:01. Switch B has priority 32768 and MAC 00:aa:bb:cc:dd:02. Which becomes the STP root bridge?
options: Switch A — bridge ID priority 4096, MAC 00:aa:bb:cc:dd:01
The switch with the most ports
The switch that booted first, always
The switch with the highest IP address
explain: The lowest bridge ID wins — priority first, then lowest MAC as tiebreaker. Switch A has the lower bridge ID (priority 4096, MAC 00:aa:bb:cc:dd:01).

q: Two switches contend to be root: A runs priority 32768 with MAC 00:00:00:00:00:0a; B runs priority 8192 with MAC 00:00:00:00:00:0b. Which switch wins the election?
options: The switch with the highest IP address
Switch B — bridge ID priority 8192, MAC 00:00:00:00:00:0b
The switch that booted first, always
The switch with the most ports
explain: The lowest bridge ID wins — priority first, then lowest MAC as tiebreaker. Switch B has the lower bridge ID (priority 8192, MAC 00:00:00:00:00:0b).

q: Switch A has priority 16384 and MAC 00:11:22:33:44:01. Switch B has priority 16384 and MAC 00:11:22:33:44:02. Which becomes the STP root bridge?
options: The switch with the highest IP address
The switch that booted first, always
Switch A — bridge ID priority 16384, MAC 00:11:22:33:44:01
The switch with the most ports
explain: The lowest bridge ID wins — priority first, then lowest MAC as tiebreaker. Switch A has the lower bridge ID (priority 16384, MAC 00:11:22:33:44:01).

q: Two switches contend to be root: A runs priority 28672 with MAC 00:de:ad:be:ef:01; B runs priority 32768 with MAC 00:de:ad:be:ef:00. Which switch wins the election?
options: The switch that booted first, always
The switch with the most ports
Switch A — bridge ID priority 28672, MAC 00:de:ad:be:ef:01
The switch with the highest IP address
explain: The lowest bridge ID wins — priority first, then lowest MAC as tiebreaker. Switch A has the lower bridge ID (priority 28672, MAC 00:de:ad:be:ef:01).

q: Two switches contend to be root: A runs priority 32768 with MAC 00:ff:00:ff:00:01; B runs priority 32768 with MAC 00:ff:00:ff:00:02. Which switch wins the election?
options: The switch with the most ports
The switch with the highest IP address
Switch A — bridge ID priority 32768, MAC 00:ff:00:ff:00:01
The switch that booted first, always
explain: The lowest bridge ID wins — priority first, then lowest MAC as tiebreaker. Switch A has the lower bridge ID (priority 32768, MAC 00:ff:00:ff:00:01).

q: A company places its Accounting PCs and its file servers in the same broadcast domain, and broadcasts from the PCs are disrupting server performance. The engineer creates VLAN 20 for Accounting and VLAN 30 for servers. What is the primary benefit achieved in this scenario?
options: Each VLAN becomes its own broadcast domain, containing broadcast traffic within that VLAN
VLANs increase the physical bandwidth of each switch port
VLANs eliminate the need for any Layer 3 device between the PCs and servers
VLANs encrypt traffic between the PCs and the servers
explain: A VLAN is a separate broadcast domain, so broadcasts from Accounting stay in VLAN 20 instead of reaching VLAN 30. VLANs do not encrypt traffic or add port bandwidth, and inter-VLAN traffic still requires a Layer 3 device.

q: An engineer needs a VLAN ID for a new department and wants it to be learnable and propagated by VTP versions 1 and 2. Which ID should the engineer choose?
options: VLAN 1006
VLAN 450
VLAN 2500
VLAN 4094
explain: VLANs 2 through 1001 are the normal range propagated by VTPv1 and VTPv2, so VLAN 450 qualifies. VLANs 1006 through 4094 are extended-range and are not propagated by VTPv1/v2.

q: While planning VLANs, an engineer tries to assign VLAN 0 and VLAN 4095 to user ports and both are rejected. Why?
options: They are reserved only for voice traffic
They are reserved for system use and cannot be assigned
They exist by default and are already in use as the native VLAN
They are extended-range VLANs that require VTP version 3
explain: VLAN 0 and VLAN 4095 are reserved for system use and cannot be configured on ports. The extended range is 1006 to 4094, which excludes both of these IDs.

q: A switch in VTP transparent mode must carry VLAN 3000 between two other switches. Which statement about this design is correct?
options: VLAN 3000 must be created locally on the transparent switch, and the switch will forward VTP advertisements without applying them
The transparent switch must be changed to VTP client mode before VLAN 3000 can be used
VLAN 3000 cannot pass through a transparent switch under any configuration
The transparent switch will learn VLAN 3000 from VTP advertisements and add it to its database
explain: A VTP transparent switch does not apply VTP updates to its own database but does forward advertisements, and extended VLANs such as 3000 must be created locally on it. A client would rely on VTP, which in v1/v2 does not propagate extended VLANs at all.

q: An IP phone and a PC share one switch port. The PC must be in VLAN 10 and phone calls must be in VLAN 50 with priority marking preserved. Which two configurations achieve this? (Choose two.)
options: Configure the port with switchport voice vlan 50
Configure the port as a trunk with only VLAN 50 allowed
Configure the PC itself to tag all its frames with VLAN 50
Configure the port with switchport access vlan 10
explain: An access port can carry one data VLAN with switchport access vlan 10 plus a separate voice VLAN with switchport voice vlan 50, and the phone tags voice traffic while passing PC data untagged. Making the port a trunk or having the PC tag as voice would break the intended data and voice separation.

q: A user reports that a Cisco IP phone plugged into a switch works, but the PC connected through the phone's switch port is in the wrong subnet. The port shows access VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 50. Where does the PC's traffic enter the switch?
options: Untagged, and the switch places it in the access (data) VLAN 10
Tagged with VLAN 50, because all traffic through a phone is tagged as voice
In the native VLAN of a trunk formed by the phone
Tagged with VLAN 10 by the phone using 802.1Q
explain: The phone tags its own voice frames with the voice VLAN and passes the attached PC's frames untagged, so the switch assigns them to the port's access VLAN. The PC traffic is not tagged by the phone and the port is not operating as a trunk.

q: An engineer configures a port with switchport mode access and switchport access vlan 15, then connects a single workstation. What traffic will this port carry?
options: Untagged traffic for VLAN 15 only
No traffic until DTP negotiates a trunk
Untagged traffic for VLAN 15 and tagged traffic for every other VLAN
Tagged traffic for all VLANs the switch knows about
explain: An access port belongs to a single VLAN and sends and receives untagged frames for that VLAN only. Carrying many tagged VLANs describes a trunk, and DTP trunk negotiation does not apply once the port is hard-set to access.

q: Two switches must exchange traffic for VLANs 10, 20, and 30 over a single link between them. Which port configuration is required on both ends of that link?
options: Routed mode with an IP address on each physical port
Trunk mode so frames for multiple VLANs can be tagged and carried
Access mode with VLAN 10 only
Voice VLAN mode with VLAN 20 assigned
explain: A trunk carries traffic for multiple VLANs over one link by tagging frames so the receiving switch can identify the VLAN. An access port carries only one VLAN, so it cannot serve all three VLANs on a single link.

q: A capture on a trunk shows a frame with an 802.1Q header inserted between the source MAC address field and the Type field, containing VLAN ID 24. What does the receiving switch do with this information?
options: It floods the frame to all VLANs because the tag makes the destination ambiguous
It changes the frame's VLAN to the native VLAN before forwarding
It uses the tag to route the frame to the default gateway for VLAN 24
It strips the tag and forwards the frame only within VLAN 24
explain: The 802.1Q tag identifies the VLAN the frame belongs to, so the receiving switch removes the tag and forwards within VLAN 24 only. Tagging is a Layer 2 function and does not by itself route the frame or change its VLAN.

q: On an 802.1Q trunk between SW1 and SW2, the native VLAN is 99 on both sides. A host in VLAN 99 sends a frame across the trunk. How is that frame transmitted?
options: Encapsulated twice to indicate it is native traffic
Tagged with VLAN ID 99 like all other VLANs
Tagged with VLAN ID 1, the default native VLAN
Untagged, because frames in the native VLAN are sent without an 802.1Q tag
explain: By default, 802.1Q sends native VLAN frames untagged, and the receiving switch assumes untagged frames belong to its native VLAN. All non-native VLANs are tagged, and the native VLAN here is 99, not 1.

q: An engineer reviews a trunk and sees this output: Gi0/1 connected trunk a-full a-1000 802.1q; VLANs allowed on trunk: 1-20,99; Native VLAN: 99; VLANs allowed and active in management domain: 1,10,20,99. Hosts in VLAN 30 cannot reach each other across this trunk. What is the cause?
options: The port speed is a-1000 instead of a fixed value
The native VLAN is set to 99 instead of 1
The trunk is using 802.1Q instead of ISL
VLAN 30 is not in the allowed list on the trunk
explain: The output lists only VLANs 1-20 and 99 as allowed on the trunk, so VLAN 30 frames are filtered before they cross. A native VLAN of 99 is valid when it matches on both ends, and 802.1Q is the correct trunking encapsulation here.

q: Users on one side of a trunk intermittently receive traffic that belongs to another VLAN, and the switches log native VLAN mismatch messages for the link. SW1 uses native VLAN 1 and SW2 uses native VLAN 99 on that trunk. What is happening to untagged frames?
options: They are dropped by both switches until the mismatch is fixed
They are automatically retagged to VLAN 99 by CDP
They are routed between VLAN 1 and VLAN 99 by the trunk itself
SW1 places untagged frames in VLAN 1 while SW2 places the same untagged frames in VLAN 99, leaking traffic between VLANs and risking STP inconsistencies
explain: Each switch assigns untagged frames to its own configured native VLAN, so a mismatch merges VLAN 1 and VLAN 99 for untagged traffic and can cause CDP warnings and spanning-tree problems. The frames are not automatically dropped, retagged, or routed by the trunk.

q: SW1 is set to switchport mode dynamic desirable and SW2 is set to switchport mode dynamic auto on the link between them, with no other trunk commands. What is the result?
options: The link is err-disabled because the modes conflict
A trunk forms, because desirable actively initiates negotiation and auto will respond
The link stays an access port because both sides must be desirable
A trunk forms only if VTP pruning is enabled
explain: Dynamic desirable actively sends DTP frames and dynamic auto will form a trunk if the other side initiates, so this pairing forms a trunk. Auto paired with auto would stay access, but that is not the pairing shown here.

q: Two newly cabled switches both have their connecting ports in switchport mode dynamic auto, and users on the far switch in VLAN 20 are unreachable. No trunk has formed. Why?
options: Auto ports actively negotiate, so a trunk should have formed and the cable must be faulty
Auto mode forms a trunk only for the native VLAN
Neither auto port initiates DTP negotiation, so the link remains an access link
DTP requires both ports to use nonegotiate mode
explain: Dynamic auto is passive: it will become a trunk only if the neighbor initiates, and with auto on both ends neither side initiates. Changing one side to desirable or hard-setting trunk would form the trunk.

q: An engineer hard-sets a port with switchport mode trunk and switchport nonegotiate. The neighboring switch port is in dynamic auto. Will a trunk form, and why?
options: Yes, because the hard-set trunk port does not send DTP but the neighbor can still detect the trunk state
Yes, because nonegotiate forces the neighbor to become a trunk via DTP
No, because a manually set trunk with nonegotiate sends no DTP, so both ends must be configured manually
No, because nonegotiate disables tagging on the port
explain: Switchport nonegotiate stops DTP frames entirely, so a dynamic auto neighbor receives nothing to trigger it and stays access; the neighbor must also be manually set to trunk. Nonegotiate does not disable 802.1Q tagging itself.

q: Which single DTP pairing will NOT result in a trunk between two Cisco switches?
options: Dynamic desirable on one side and dynamic desirable on the other
Dynamic auto on one side and dynamic auto on the other
Manual trunk on one side and dynamic desirable on the other
Dynamic desirable on one side and dynamic auto on the other
explain: Auto/auto never forms a trunk because neither side initiates DTP negotiation. Every other pairing listed includes at least one side that actively initiates or is hard-set as a trunk.

q: In a VTP domain, an engineer creates VLAN 40 on the VTP server. A switch in VTP client mode and a switch in VTP transparent mode are connected. What happens on each switch?
options: The transparent switch learns VLAN 40 and the client rejects it
Both switches learn VLAN 40 automatically from the advertisement
Neither switch learns it until VLAN 40 is created locally on each
The client learns VLAN 40, while the transparent switch ignores the update for its own database but forwards the advertisement
explain: VTP clients synchronize their VLAN database from server advertisements, while transparent switches do not apply advertisements to their own database but do forward them. Creating the VLAN locally is required only on the transparent switch.

q: A refurbished switch that was previously used in a lab is added to a production VTP domain as a client with a higher configuration revision number than the server, and production VLANs disappear across the domain. What caused this, and how is it prevented? (Choose two.)
options: The switch was in transparent mode, which always deletes VLANs
Reset the revision number before deployment by changing the VTP domain name or switching to transparent mode and back
Production VLANs were removed by STP reconvergence triggered by the new switch
The client overwrote the domain database because VTP trusts the highest revision number regardless of server or client role
explain: VTP synchronizes to the highest revision number in the domain even if it comes from a client, so a stale lab database can overwrite production VLANs. Resetting the revision number first, for example by toggling the domain name or using transparent mode, prevents the overwrite.

q: An engineer must create VLAN 25 named SALES on a switch and verify it exists before assigning ports. Which command sequence and verification are correct?
options: vlan create 25 SALES in privileged EXEC, verified with show interfaces trunk
vlan 25 in global configuration, then name SALES in VLAN configuration, verified with show vlan brief
switchport vlan 25 in global configuration, verified with show trunk
set vlan 25 SALES in interface configuration, verified with show running-config only
explain: VLANs are created in global configuration with the vlan command and optionally named in VLAN configuration mode, and show vlan brief lists VLANs and their assigned ports. The other command forms are not valid IOS syntax for creating a VLAN.

q: An engineer runs a command and sees: VLAN Name Status Ports; 1 default active Gi0/3, Gi0/4; 10 DATA active Gi0/1; 20 VOICE active; 1002 fddi-default act/unsup. A PC plugged into Gi0/2 cannot be found in the list and gets no connectivity to VLAN 10 resources. What does the output indicate?
options: Gi0/2 is shut down by STP
Gi0/2 is operating as a trunk and trunks never appear correctly
Gi0/2 has not been assigned to VLAN 10, because only Gi0/1 is listed under VLAN 10 in the output
VLAN 10 is suspended and must be reactivated
explain: Show vlan brief lists each access port under its assigned VLAN, and Gi0/1 is the only port shown for VLAN 10, so Gi0/2 was never assigned to VLAN 10. A trunk would also be absent from this list, but nothing in the output indicates a trunk, shutdown, or a suspended VLAN 10, which shows as active.

q: An engineer checks a link and sees: Port Mode Encapsulation Status Native vlan; Gi0/1 on 802.1q trunking 99; Port Vlans allowed on trunk; Gi0/1 10,20,99. The far side reports native VLAN 1. What problem must be fixed first?
options: VLAN 10 must be added to the allowed list
The encapsulation must be changed to ISL
The native VLANs do not match, so untagged traffic will be placed in different VLANs on each side
The port mode must be changed to desirable
explain: Show interfaces trunk shows this side uses native VLAN 99 while the neighbor uses 1, so untagged frames are classified differently on each end and must be made to match. VLAN 10 is already allowed, and the mode on plus 802.1Q encapsulation are both working as shown.

q: An engineer troubleshoots a port that should be a trunk and sees: Name: Gi0/2; Switchport: Enabled; Administrative Mode: dynamic auto; Operational Mode: static access; Administrative Trunking Encapsulation: dot1q; Negotiation of Trunking: On. The neighbor is hard-set to trunk with nonegotiate. Why is this port not trunking?
options: Because the neighbor sends no DTP frames due to nonegotiate, so this auto port never receives a negotiation to respond to
Because dot1q encapsulation prevents trunking with a hard-set neighbor
Because dynamic auto cannot become a trunk under any circumstance
Because Switchport is enabled, which forces access mode
explain: Show interfaces switchport shows the port is operationally static access and administratively dynamic auto, and a nonegotiate neighbor sends no DTP, so the passive auto side never triggers. Hard-setting this side to trunk as well resolves it, whereas auto can trunk when a neighbor actively negotiates.

q: A help-desk change moves a user PC to a new desk. The switch port must carry only VLAN 15, untagged, and must not be able to become a trunk even if the attached device requests it. Which configuration is best?
options: switchport mode access and switchport access vlan 15
switchport mode dynamic desirable and switchport access vlan 15
switchport mode trunk and switchport trunk allowed vlan 15
switchport voice vlan 15 only
explain: Switchport mode access fixes the port as a non-trunking access port in VLAN 15 and ignores trunk requests. Dynamic desirable would actively try to form a trunk, which is the opposite of the requirement.

q: After a change, a trunk between two switches carries VLANs 10 and 20 but a newly added VLAN 30 does not pass, even though VLAN 30 exists on both switches. The trunk was configured with switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20. What is the correct fix?
options: Use switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30 to add VLAN 30 without removing VLANs 10 and 20
Remove the trunk and recreate it as an access port in VLAN 30
Re-enter switchport trunk allowed vlan 30, which replaces the list with only VLAN 30
Change the native VLAN to 30 so VLAN 30 passes untagged by itself
explain: The add keyword appends a VLAN to the existing allowed list, preserving VLANs 10 and 20. Re-entering the allowed command without add replaces the entire list and would break the VLANs that currently work.

q: A router-on-a-stick design must route between VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24) and VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24) over one physical router interface. Which router configuration is correct for VLAN 10?
options: interface Vlan10 on the router with ip routing enabled
interface Gi0/0.10 with switchport access vlan 10 configured on the router
interface Gi0/0 with encapsulation dot1Q 10 and two IP addresses in both subnets
interface Gi0/0.10 with encapsulation dot1Q 10 and ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0, with the physical interface enabled
explain: Router-on-a-stick uses logical subinterfaces, each with encapsulation dot1Q matching its VLAN and that VLAN's gateway address, while the physical interface is simply enabled with no IP address. Switchport and SVI commands belong on a Layer 3 switch, not on this router subinterface design.

q: In a router-on-a-stick deployment, hosts in the native VLAN 99 lose connectivity while tagged VLANs 10 and 20 work. The subinterface for VLAN 99 was configured with encapsulation dot1Q 99 and no other keyword. What is missing?
options: DTP negotiation on the router subinterface
An IP address on the physical interface in the VLAN 99 subnet as well
A second physical link dedicated to the native VLAN
The native keyword, so the router expects untagged frames for VLAN 99 to be associated with that subinterface
explain: When a subinterface serves the native VLAN, encapsulation dot1Q 99 native tells the router that untagged frames belong to that subinterface. Without it the router expects VLAN 99 frames to arrive tagged, while the switch sends native VLAN frames untagged.

q: A Layer 3 switch must route between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 using SVIs. VLANs and SVIs are created with IP addresses, but hosts still cannot route between VLANs. The switch shows both SVIs up/up. What command is most likely missing?
options: switchport mode trunk on each SVI
encapsulation dot1Q on each SVI
spanning-tree portfast on the SVIs
ip routing in global configuration
explain: A Layer 3 switch does not route between SVIs until ip routing is enabled globally, even if the SVIs are up and addressed. SVIs are logical Layer 3 interfaces and do not take switchport, encapsulation, or PortFast commands.

q: An SVI for VLAN 40 on a Layer 3 switch stays up/down even though it has an IP address and is not shut down. VLAN 40 exists in the VLAN database. What is the most likely remaining condition?
options: STP has placed the SVI itself into blocking state
The VLAN name was not configured
No active Layer 2 port is assigned to VLAN 40 and no trunk carrying VLAN 40 is up, so the SVI has no active link to keep it up
The SVI needs a default gateway configured on the switch itself
explain: An SVI stays up only when its VLAN exists and at least one Layer 2 port in that VLAN (access or trunk) is up and in spanning-tree forwarding. A missing VLAN name or STP state on the SVI itself does not cause up/down.

q: A growing campus replaces router-on-a-stick with a Layer 3 switch for inter-VLAN routing. Which advantage is the main driver for this change?
options: The Layer 3 switch removes the single-link bottleneck and routes between SVIs at switch hardware speed without sending all inter-VLAN traffic to an external router
The Layer 3 switch eliminates the need for VLANs entirely
The Layer 3 switch allows hosts in different VLANs to communicate without any IP addressing
The Layer 3 switch makes STP unnecessary on access ports
explain: SVI routing on a Layer 3 switch forwards inter-VLAN traffic in hardware across the switch backplane instead of hair-pinning everything over one router link. VLANs, IP addressing, and STP on Layer 2 ports are all still required.

q: Which two statements correctly describe inter-VLAN routing choices on the switch side? (Choose two.)
options: A routed port on a Layer 3 switch is a physical port with no switchport and its own IP address, not tied to a VLAN
Router-on-a-stick requires ip routing to be enabled on the switch
An SVI requires a dedicated physical port for every host in the VLAN
An SVI provides the default gateway interface for hosts in its VLAN on a Layer 3 switch
explain: An SVI is the Layer 3 gateway for its VLAN, and a routed port (no switchport) is a separate physical Layer 3 interface with its own address. An SVI serves the whole VLAN without per-host ports, and ip routing for router-on-a-stick is a router function, not a switch requirement.

q: Three switches form a triangle. SW-A has priority 24576 for VLAN 10, SW-B has priority 32768, and SW-C has priority 32768 with the lowest MAC address of the three. Which switch becomes root for VLAN 10 in PVST+?
options: All three share the root role for load balancing
SW-B, because it was listed first with the default priority
SW-A, because it has the lowest bridge priority, which is compared before MAC address
SW-C, because the lowest MAC always wins
explain: Root election compares bridge ID, which is priority first and MAC address only as a tiebreaker, so SW-A's lower priority of 24576 wins. SW-C's lower MAC would matter only if the priorities tied, as they do between SW-B and SW-C.

q: An engineer examines STP output: Bridge ID Priority 32778 (priority 32768 sys-id-ext 10); Address 001a.2b3c.4d5e; Root ID Priority 32778; Address 001a.2b3c.4d5e; This bridge is the root. What does this output prove?
options: This switch is the root because its port is in blocking state
This switch learned the root from a neighbor with the same address
This switch is itself the root bridge for VLAN 10, because its bridge ID matches the root ID
The root bridge cannot be determined from this output
explain: When the Root ID in show spanning-tree matches the local Bridge ID and the output states this bridge is the root, the local switch won the election for that VLAN. The sys-id-ext of 10 shows this instance is for VLAN 10 under PVST+.

q: A non-root switch has two uplinks: Gi0/1 with a path cost of 4 to the root and Gi0/2 with a path cost of 19 to the root, with no other differences. Which port becomes the root port and why?
options: Both ports become root ports for redundancy
Gi0/1, because the root port is the port with the lowest path cost to the root bridge
Neither, until an IP address is assigned to one uplink
Gi0/2, because a higher cost is preferred
explain: Each non-root switch selects exactly one root port, the one offering the lowest cumulative path cost to the root, which is Gi0/1 at cost 4. The other uplink takes a non-root role such as designated or alternate.

q: On a single switch-to-switch segment, both switches agree SW1 is closer to the root. SW1's port on that segment forwards traffic for the segment while SW2 already has a root port elsewhere. What role does SW1's port on this segment hold?
options: Alternate port
Backup port on a shared segment to itself
Root port
Designated port, because it is the port on the segment responsible for forwarding toward and from the root for that segment
explain: Every segment has one designated port that forwards for that segment, chosen from the switch with the best path to the root on that segment. A switch has only one root port total, and it points toward the root, not out to a downstream segment.

q: In Rapid PVST+, a switch port that provides an alternative path to the root but is currently discarding traffic to prevent a loop holds which role?
options: Alternate port
Edge port
Designated port
Root port
explain: The alternate role in RSTP-based Rapid PVST+ is a blocked (discarding) backup path to the root on a non-root switch. Root and designated ports forward, and an edge port connects to an end device rather than offering an alternate path to the root.

q: A legacy STP port cycles through listening and learning before forwarding, causing a long delay, while a Rapid PVST+ port moves from discarding directly through learning to forwarding much faster. Which RSTP change explains the faster behavior?
options: RSTP elects two root bridges so ports never need to wait
RSTP uses only discarding, learning, and forwarding states and can use a proposal and agreement handshake instead of relying only on timers
RSTP removes the learning state entirely
RSTP forwards immediately on all ports regardless of topology
explain: RSTP collapses blocking, listening, and disabled into discarding, keeping learning and forwarding, and speeds convergence with proposal/agreement exchanges. It does not remove learning or forward blindly on every port, which would create loops.

q: A workstation port takes about 30 seconds to start passing traffic after the PC boots, delaying DHCP. The port connects only to that single PC and no switch will ever be attached. Which feature should be enabled on this port?
options: Root guard, so the PC cannot become root
UDLD, so the link is checked for unidirectional failures
PortFast, so the port transitions immediately to forwarding at link-up
BPDU Guard alone, with normal STP timers left in place
explain: PortFast lets an edge port skip the listening and learning delays and forward immediately, which fixes slow DHCP on a single-host port. BPDU Guard alone does not speed the transition, and root guard is meant for ports where a root bridge should never appear, not for speeding host access.

q: A PortFast-enabled access port goes into err-disabled state the moment a user connects a small unmanaged switch to it. Which feature caused the shutdown and why?
options: Root guard, because the unmanaged switch advertised a lower priority
STP cost recalculation, because the new switch changed the path cost
Loop guard, because BPDUs stopped arriving on the port
BPDU Guard, because the PortFast port received a BPDU and BPDU Guard err-disables the port to protect the topology
explain: BPDU Guard is paired with PortFast so that if a BPDU arrives on an edge port, indicating a switch was attached, the port is err-disabled. Loop guard reacts to missing BPDUs, the opposite condition, and root guard puts a port into a root-inconsistent blocking state rather than err-disabling it.

q: An engineer wants to ensure a distribution switch port facing a downstream access switch never accepts that access switch as the root bridge, even if it is configured with a superior priority. At awareness level, which feature fits?
options: PortFast on the distribution port
EtherChannel guard on both switches
BPDU filtering on the access switch uplink
Root guard on the distribution port, which moves the port to root-inconsistent if a superior BPDU arrives
explain: Root guard protects the current root's position by blocking a port that receives a superior BPDU until that BPDU stops. PortFast is for edge host ports and BPDU filtering would hide BPDUs entirely, neither of which enforces root placement on a switch-to-switch port.

q: Which two statements correctly pair an STP protection feature with the condition it addresses? (Choose two.)
options: Loop guard prevents a non-designated port from transitioning to forwarding when it stops receiving BPDUs, protecting against unidirectional link failures
Root guard err-disables a port when any BPDU is received on a PortFast port
Loop guard speeds up host ports by skipping listening and learning
BPDU Guard err-disables a PortFast edge port that receives a BPDU
explain: Loop guard addresses the loss of BPDUs on a non-designated port, and BPDU Guard err-disables an edge PortFast port that unexpectedly receives a BPDU. Root guard uses a root-inconsistent state rather than err-disable, and skipping STP states describes PortFast, not loop guard.

q: An engineer replaces classic PVST+ with Rapid PVST+ across a campus. Users notice that after a topology change, reconvergence that previously took up to 50 seconds now completes in a few seconds or less. What is the main reason?
options: Rapid PVST+ elects the root based on IP address instead of bridge ID
Rapid PVST+ floods all traffic during convergence so no port ever blocks
Rapid PVST+ disables STP on access ports by default
Rapid PVST+ uses discarding, learning, and forwarding states with rapid proposal and agreement exchanges instead of timer-based listening and learning on every port
explain: Rapid PVST+ retains per-VLAN spanning tree but converges rapidly because ports negotiate roles with proposal/agreement messages rather than waiting out max age and forward delay timers. It still runs STP on ports and still elects roots by bridge ID.

q: A switch calculates STP path cost using the classic short method. A 100 Mbps link and a 1 Gbps link connect it toward the root. Which costs are assigned to those links?
options: 100 Mbps cost 4 and 1 Gbps cost 19
Both links cost 1 because they are full-duplex
100 Mbps cost 19 and 1 Gbps cost 4
100 Mbps cost 10 and 1 Gbps cost 1
explain: Under the classic STP cost table, 100 Mbps is cost 19 and 1 Gbps is cost 4, so the gigabit link is preferred toward the root. Duplex does not change the bandwidth-based cost values.

q: Two switches must form an LACP EtherChannel. SW1 uses channel-group 1 mode active and SW2 uses channel-group 1 mode passive. What is the result?
options: A channel forms only after PAgP is also enabled
The ports are err-disabled because active and passive conflict
A channel forms, because active initiates LACP negotiation and passive will respond
No channel forms, because both sides must be active
explain: LACP active actively negotiates and passive responds, so active/passive is a valid forming pair. Passive/passive would fail because neither side initiates, which is not the case here.

q: An EtherChannel configured with LACP passive on both switches never bundles, and the individual ports stay in a standalone state. What is the fix that keeps LACP in use?
options: Change both sides to passive desirable
Enable DTP on the member ports
Change at least one side to active so negotiation is initiated
Set both sides to PAgP auto instead and keep the LACP commands
explain: With passive on both ends, neither switch sends LACP negotiation first, so no channel forms; making at least one side active fixes it. Passive desirable is not an LACP mode, and DTP negotiates trunks, not EtherChannel bundles.

q: A legacy design uses PAgP between two Cisco switches. SW1 is set to desirable and SW2 is set to auto. What happens, and how does it compare to auto on both sides?
options: Neither combination can ever form a PAgP channel
Desirable/auto forms a channel because desirable initiates, while auto/auto would not form because neither side initiates
Both combinations form channels in exactly the same way
Desirable/auto does not form, but auto/auto does form
explain: PAgP mirrors the DTP pattern: desirable actively negotiates and auto responds, so desirable/auto bundles, while auto/auto never starts negotiation and stays unbundled. Only the first statement captures both outcomes correctly.

q: An engineer audits an EtherChannel and sees: Group Port-channel Protocol Ports; 1 Po1(SU) LACP Gi0/1(P) Gi0/2(P). A second group shows: 2 Po2(SD) PAgP Gi0/3(I) Gi0/4(I). What does the comparison show?
options: Both groups are bundled and passing traffic
Group 2 is bundled because its ports show the (I) flag
Group 1 is bundled and in use with LACP, while group 2 is down with its ports operating as individual standalone links under PAgP
Group 1 uses PAgP and group 2 uses LACP
explain: In show etherchannel summary, (P) means a port is bundled in the port-channel and SU means the Layer 2 channel is in use, while (I) means standalone and SD means the Layer 2 channel is down. Group 1 is therefore healthy with LACP and group 2 is not bundled under PAgP.

q: A single large file transfer between one server pair uses an EtherChannel of four 1 Gbps links but never exceeds about 1 Gbps. Management expects 4 Gbps for that one flow. What should the engineer explain?
options: EtherChannel load balancing hashes flow attributes such as source and destination addresses, so a single flow is pinned to one member link and gets only that link's bandwidth
EtherChannel is broken and must be reconfigured as a trunk
The transfer is limited because LACP always reserves three links as standby
Increasing the STP cost on three links will spread the single flow across all four
explain: EtherChannel distributes different flows across member links by hashing addresses or ports, but any one flow follows a single link, so it cannot exceed 1 Gbps here. LACP does not hold the other links as standby in a bundled channel, and STP cost is unrelated to per-flow hashing.

q: An engineer must build an EtherChannel that itself carries an IP address and routes traffic, rather than acting as a Layer 2 trunk. Which configuration approach is correct?
options: Assign a separate IP address to each member port
Enable switchport mode trunk and place the IP address on a member port
Put no switchport on the member ports and the port-channel, and assign the IP address to the port-channel interface
Configure the port-channel as an access port in one VLAN and add a secondary IP address
explain: A Layer 3 EtherChannel is built by making the physical members and the port-channel routed interfaces with no switchport, then addressing the port-channel itself. Addressing individual members breaks the bundle concept, and a Layer 2 trunk port-channel uses SVIs, not a member-port IP address.

q: An EtherChannel bundle will not form between two switches. Investigation shows Gi0/1 on SW1 is allowed VLANs 10,20 on its trunk while the matching member on SW2 is allowed VLANs 10,20,30, and all other settings match. Why does the bundle fail?
options: The allowed VLAN lists must be in descending order
LACP cannot operate if more than two VLANs are allowed
EtherChannel requires the native VLAN to be VLAN 1 on both sides
Member ports must have identical settings, including the same allowed VLANs, speed, duplex, and mode, or the port-channel will not bundle consistently
explain: EtherChannel members must agree on parameters such as allowed VLANs, speed, duplex, and switchport mode; a mismatch suspends or prevents bundling. The native VLAN does not have to be VLAN 1 as long as it matches, and the number or order of VLANs is not the issue.

q: A network technician uses a protocol analyzer and notices a multicast frame from a Cisco switch advertising its device ID, platform, IOS version, and the port it was sent from, without any request being made. Which protocol and behavior is this?
options: LLDP, which is an open standard sent only on request
VTP, which advertises VLAN database revisions
DTP, which advertises trunking capability only
CDP, a Cisco proprietary Layer 2 protocol that periodically advertises neighbor information and is enabled by default on Cisco devices
explain: CDP is Cisco proprietary, operates at Layer 2, and periodically sends unsolicited advertisements containing device, port, platform, and version details, enabled by default on Cisco gear. LLDP is the vendor-neutral standard, and DTP and VTP advertise trunk and VLAN information respectively, not device identity in this way.

q: A mixed-vendor environment contains Cisco and non-Cisco switches that must discover each other as neighbors. Which protocol should be enabled and why?
options: CDP, because it is supported by all vendors
VTP, because it propagates neighbor tables
PAgP, because it discovers neighbors across vendors
LLDP, the IEEE 802.1AB vendor-neutral standard, because CDP is Cisco proprietary
explain: LLDP is the open IEEE standard that any vendor can implement, making it suitable for mixed environments. CDP works only on Cisco (and licensed) devices, and PAgP and VTP are for EtherChannel negotiation and VLAN propagation, not neighbor discovery.

q: An engineer runs a neighbor command and sees: Capability Codes: R - Router, S - Switch; Device ID Local Intrfce Holdtme Capability Platform Port ID; SW2 Gig 0/1 154 S I WS-C3560 Gig 0/2. What command produced this and what was learned?
options: show cdp neighbors, and the local Gi0/1 connects to SW2 on its Gi0/2, which is a switch
show interfaces trunk, and Gi0/1 is a routed port
show vlan brief, and SW2 belongs to VLAN 154
show lldp neighbors, and the neighbor is a non-Cisco router
explain: The Capability Codes and Device ID layout is show cdp neighbors output, showing local Gi0/1 connected to switch SW2's Gi0/2 port. The holdtime value of 154 is a timer in seconds, not a VLAN, and LLDP output uses a different format.

q: Which two statements about CDP and LLDP security and scope are correct? (Choose two.)
options: CDP and LLDP information is visible only to directly connected neighbors, not routed across Layer 3 hops
LLDP should be enabled on internet-facing ports so attackers can verify the device type
CDP encrypts its advertisements by default to prevent information disclosure
Both protocols advertise detailed device information, so they should be disabled on ports facing untrusted networks
explain: CDP and LLDP operate at Layer 2 between direct neighbors and disclose platform and version details, so best practice disables them toward untrusted networks. Neither protocol encrypts advertisements by default, and exposing them on internet-facing ports increases risk rather than reducing it.

q: After a desk move, a PC gets an IP address in 192.168.20.0/24 but the user needs resources in VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24). The switch port shows switchport access vlan 20 and the PC's MAC appears in VLAN 20. What is the correct fix?
options: Add VLAN 10 to the port as a voice VLAN
Convert the port to a trunk so it can carry both VLANs to the PC
Change the PC's default gateway to the VLAN 20 SVI and leave the port unchanged
Change the port to switchport access vlan 10 so the PC is placed in the intended VLAN
explain: The PC is simply assigned to the wrong access VLAN; moving the port to VLAN 10 places it in the correct broadcast domain and subnet. Keeping it in VLAN 20 with a different gateway does not put the PC in VLAN 10, and a standard PC does not need a trunk or a voice VLAN assignment.

q: A link between a switch (hard-set to 100 Mbps full-duplex) and a workstation (left on autonegotiation) is slow and the switch logs late collisions and FCS errors on the workstation side. The workstation negotiated half-duplex. What is the root cause?
options: The workstation is in the wrong VLAN
A duplex mismatch: when one side is hard-set to full-duplex, autonegotiation on the other side cannot detect duplex and falls back to half-duplex
STP placed the workstation port into listening state permanently
A native VLAN mismatch on the access port
explain: If one end is manually set to full-duplex, the auto side can sense speed but not duplex and defaults to half-duplex, producing late collisions and FCS errors. The fix is to match settings on both ends, either both auto or both hard-set identically.

q: Two switches are linked by a working trunk. Hosts in VLAN 10 communicate across it, but hosts in VLAN 40 on the far switch are isolated, and VLAN 40 exists and is active on both switches. The trunk on SW1 was configured months ago with an explicit allowed list. What is the most likely cause?
options: STP blocks any VLAN above 39 by default
VLAN 40 was never added to the trunk's allowed VLAN list on SW1, so its frames are pruned from the trunk
The switches need VTP server mode on both ends for a trunk to carry more than one VLAN
VLAN 40 must be made the native VLAN before it can cross any trunk
explain: An explicit switchport trunk allowed vlan list filters which VLANs may cross, and a later-created VLAN is not automatically added to a manually restricted list. No rule requires a VLAN to be native, both switches to be VTP servers, or caps VLAN numbers for trunks.

q: An IP phone displays the correct voice VLAN and can place calls, but the PC behind the phone receives an address from the voice subnet instead of the data subnet. The port configuration shows switchport access vlan 50 and switchport voice vlan 50. What is wrong?
options: The port must be changed to a trunk with native VLAN 50
Both VLANs were set to 50, so the data (access) VLAN must be changed to the intended data VLAN while the voice VLAN stays 50
CDP must be disabled so the phone stops learning a VLAN
The voice VLAN must be removed so the phone uses the access VLAN for calls
explain: The access VLAN defines where untagged PC data goes, and here it was mistakenly also set to 50, the voice VLAN, so the PC lands in the voice subnet. Correcting the access VLAN to the data VLAN restores separation while leaving voice service untouched.

q: Which two benefits do VLANs provide in a campus design beyond simply separating users? (Choose two.)
options: VLANs automatically increase the speed of every access port
VLANs provide a security boundary that can be enforced with Layer 3 policies between groups
VLANs remove the need for spanning tree on redundant links
VLANs let logical groupings be applied regardless of physical location, so a user keeps the same VLAN when moving within the switched network
explain: VLANs decouple logical membership from physical location and create boundaries where ACLs and firewall policy can be applied between groups. They do not change port speed, and redundant Layer 2 links still require spanning tree regardless of VLAN count.

q: An engineer configures a new switch port for a user and issues switchport mode dynamic desirable. The attached device is a normal PC that never sends DTP. What operational mode will the port use, and what risk does the setting introduce?
options: It will operate as a routed port because DTP failed
It will operate as an access port, but the desirable setting could let an attacker device negotiate a trunk and reach other VLANs
It will operate as a trunk and immediately expose all VLANs to the PC
It will be err-disabled because a PC cannot answer DTP
explain: With no DTP response from the PC, a dynamic desirable port falls back to access operation, but leaving DTP active on user ports risks VLAN hopping if an attacker negotiates a trunk. Best practice is to hard-set user ports to access mode.

q: A trunk is configured so that VLAN 1 is not the native VLAN; instead VLAN 999, an unused VLAN with no hosts or SVI, is set as native on both ends with switchport trunk native vlan 999. What is the security purpose of this design?
options: It moves untagged control and stray traffic into a dead-end VLAN, reducing VLAN hopping exposure associated with using VLAN 1 as native
It disables CDP and DTP advertisements on the trunk
It encrypts untagged traffic using VLAN 999
It prevents any tagged traffic from crossing the trunk
explain: Using an unused dedicated native VLAN keeps untagged frames out of a production or default VLAN and mitigates double-tagging style VLAN hopping that targets VLAN 1 as native. It does not encrypt traffic, stop control protocols by itself, or block tagged VLANs.

q: An engineer verifies a port-channel and sees: Port-channel1 is up, line protocol is up; Hardware is EtherChannel; Members: Gi0/1 up, Gi0/2 up; but user traffic for VLAN 20 fails while VLAN 10 works over the same bundle. The port-channel is a trunk with allowed VLANs 10,20 on SW1 and allowed VLAN 10 only on SW2's port-channel. What is the issue?
options: The trunk allowed VLAN lists on the two port-channels are inconsistent, so VLAN 20 is filtered on SW2's side
VLAN 20 must be the native VLAN on both port-channels
The EtherChannel itself is down and must be rebuilt
LACP cannot bundle ports if two VLANs are allowed
explain: The bundle is up with both members up, so the failure is per-VLAN filtering: SW2's port-channel allows only VLAN 10, so VLAN 20 frames are not carried there. EtherChannel trunks routinely carry multiple VLANs and do not require the affected VLAN to be native.

q: On a switch, an engineer needs to confirm whether a specific uplink is currently operating as a trunk, which VLANs are allowed, and what the native VLAN is, all in one command. Which command provides exactly this summary?
options: show cdp neighbors detail
show etherchannel summary
show interfaces trunk
show vlan brief
explain: Show interfaces trunk lists each trunking port with its mode, encapsulation, status, native VLAN, and allowed VLAN lists in one view. Show vlan brief omits trunk details such as the native VLAN and allowed lists.

q: Which two actions correctly harden or correctly configure a trunk link between two switches? (Choose two.)
options: Allow every VLAN ever created, including unused VLANs, to reduce configuration effort
Set both ends with switchport mode trunk so the trunk does not depend on DTP negotiation
Set the same native VLAN on both ends with switchport trunk native vlan
Set one end to dynamic auto and the other end to dynamic auto and rely on DTP
explain: Hard-setting trunk mode and matching the native VLAN on both ends produces a deterministic, consistent trunk. Auto/auto never forms a trunk, and allowing unused VLANs widens the attack and failure surface instead of following least-privilege trunk configuration.

q: A Rapid PVST+ topology shows a port in the Designated role with state FWD on one switch and a port in the Alternate role with state BLK on the peer segment toward the root. An engineer disconnects the current root port link. What should happen to the alternate port?
options: It becomes an access port in VLAN 1
It err-disables to protect the topology
It transitions to forwarding, taking over as the new path to the root, typically very quickly under RSTP rules
It stays blocking forever until the switch is reloaded
explain: The alternate port is a precomputed backup path to the root, so when the root port fails, RSTP can promote the alternate port to root and move it to forwarding rapidly. It does not stay blocked, change to an access port, or err-disable on a link failure.

q: An engineer wants a specific distribution switch to reliably become the root for VLAN 10 without depending on MAC address tiebreakers against an identical default priority elsewhere. Which configuration is most deterministic?
options: spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096 on the distribution switch, giving it a clearly lower priority than the default 32768
Enable PortFast on all its ports so it is elected first
Leave the priority at default and lower its STP port cost on access ports
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 61440 on the distribution switch
explain: Root election prefers the lowest priority, so setting 4096 (a valid multiple of 4096) makes this switch deterministically preferred over default-priority switches. Raising its priority to 61440 would make it less likely to become root, and PortFast and port cost do not decide which switch wins the root election.

q: An administrator enables LLDP on a switch with the global command lldp run, but a connected non-Cisco phone still does not appear as a neighbor on one interface, while it does on others. The interface has lldp transmit disabled from an earlier security change. What does this illustrate?
options: The phone must be placed in the voice VLAN before LLDP can operate
LLDP requires CDP to be enabled on the same interface to function
LLDP can be controlled per interface for transmit and receive separately, and a per-interface transmit disable blocks advertisements on that port despite the global enable
LLDP neighbors appear only after 24 hours of uptime
explain: LLDP is enabled globally with lldp run but can be tuned per interface with no lldp transmit or no lldp receive, and the leftover transmit disable explains this single port. LLDP is independent of CDP and does not require a voice VLAN to exchange TLVs.

q: A new branch switch is added with default settings and connected to an existing switch. Without any configuration, the existing switch can already see the new switch's hostname, platform, and connecting port in its neighbor table. Which default behavior explains this?
options: LLDP is enabled by default on all Cisco switch ports
VTP is enabled by default and shares neighbor tables
CDP is enabled by default on Cisco devices, both globally and on interfaces, so neighbors are discovered automatically
DTP shares hostname and platform information between trunk neighbors
explain: Cisco devices run CDP by default, so a newly connected Cisco switch is immediately visible with show cdp neighbors including its platform and port. LLDP on IOS switches is typically not enabled by default and must be turned on with lldp run, and neither VTP nor DTP carries this neighbor identity information.

q: An engineer reviews output for a user port: Gi0/5 connected 20 a-full a-100; status shows VLAN 20, full duplex negotiated, speed 100 Mbps. The user PC is capable of 1 Gbps and the cable and switch port support 1 Gbps, but the PC NIC was hard-set to 100 Mbps full-duplex years ago. A second user on a correctly configured auto port reaches 1 Gbps. What is the best action for the first port?
options: Leave it, because 100 Mbps is the maximum for any access port in VLAN 20
Set both the switch port and the PC NIC to autonegotiation so they can negotiate 1 Gbps full-duplex consistently
Change the PC to VLAN 10, which supports gigabit speeds
Hard-set the switch port to 1000 Mbps full-duplex while leaving the PC at 100 Mbps
explain: Matching autonegotiation on both ends lets the link negotiate its highest common capability, 1 Gbps full-duplex. Hard-setting mismatched speeds would prevent link establishment, and VLAN membership has no bearing on negotiated port speed.

q: Which two configurations are required on the switch side to support inter-VLAN routing for VLANs 10 and 20 on a Layer 3 switch, assuming the VLANs and host ports already exist? (Choose two.)
options: Create interface vlan 10 and interface vlan 20, assign each its gateway IP address, and ensure each is no shutdown
Configure every access port as a trunk
Assign an IP address directly to every access port in VLANs 10 and 20
Enable ip routing globally on the switch
explain: Layer 3 switching needs addressed, enabled SVIs for each VLAN plus global ip routing so the switch forwards between them. Access ports stay as access ports and are never given individual IP addresses.

q: A design requires an EtherChannel of exactly the mode pair that forms a PAgP channel but would fail if the same word pair were used with LACP auto modes. An engineer proposes desirable on one side and auto on the other for PAgP, and separately passive on both sides for LACP. How should this proposal be judged for the PAgP bundle alone?
options: The PAgP bundle will fail, because both sides must be desirable
The PAgP bundle will form only if the ports are also access ports
The PAgP bundle will form, because desirable initiates negotiation and auto responds
The PAgP bundle will be blocked by STP permanently
explain: For PAgP, desirable/auto is a forming pair because one side initiates and the other responds. Requiring desirable on both sides is too strict, since desirable/desirable also works but is not the only valid combination.

q: A spanning-tree review for VLAN 30 shows every switch using the default priority, and the root turns out to be an old access switch in a wiring closet instead of the intended core switch. No priorities were ever configured. What determined the root, and what is the lesson?
options: The switch with the highest MAC address won, so MAC addresses should be changed on the core
The first switch to boot always remains root regardless of bridge ID
The switch with the most ports won because port count is part of the bridge ID
With all priorities equal at 32768 plus the VLAN extension, the switch with the lowest MAC address won by tiebreaker, showing why the core should be given an intentionally lower priority
explain: Bridge ID comparison falls through to the lowest MAC address when priorities tie, which let an arbitrary old access switch become root. The fix is to configure an intentionally low priority on the intended core rather than relying on the tiebreaker.

q: An engineer reviews EtherChannel settings and sees this output: EtherChannel Load-Balancing Configuration: src-dst-ip; EtherChannel Load-Balancing Addresses Used Per-Protocol: Non-IP: src-dst-mac; IPv4: src-dst-ip. Two servers in the same subnet pair exchange many separate flows over the bundle. How are those flows distributed?
options: Only non-IP traffic uses the bundle and IP traffic uses a single member
All flows between that one source and destination IP pair hash to the same member link, so distribution improves only when different address pairs are involved
Each packet is sprayed round-robin across all member links regardless of addresses
The hash ignores IP addresses and uses only the ingress port number
explain: With src-dst-ip balancing, the hash is based on the source and destination IP pair, so flows sharing the same pair follow the same member link. Per-packet round-robin is not how EtherChannel balances, because it would risk out-of-order delivery within a flow.

q: A switch port configured with channel-group 5 mode on is paired with a neighbor configured for LACP active, and no EtherChannel forms. The engineer expected on mode to negotiate. What is the correct explanation?
options: On mode requires VTP to complete the negotiation
On mode is another name for LACP active
On mode forces the ports into a channel without any negotiation protocol, so it must be paired with on mode on the other side and will not respond to LACP
On mode forms a channel only if DTP is set to desirable
explain: Mode on statically forces a channel with no LACP or PAgP negotiation at all, so an LACP active neighbor receives no LACP from this side and cannot bundle. Both ends must use compatible settings, on with on, or a matching negotiated pair.

q: A small office deploys a single access point that is configured directly through its own CLI and continues to forward traffic with no controller present. Which architecture is in use?
options: A lightweight AP that has lost its controller
An autonomous AP operating as a standalone device
A lightweight AP in monitor mode
A FlexConnect AP switching traffic locally
explain: An autonomous AP contains the full control and forwarding logic and is configured individually, so it works without a WLC. A lightweight AP depends on a WLC for configuration and management, so standalone operation rules it out.

q: Branch clients are served by a lightweight AP in local mode when its CAPWAP tunnel to the central WLC fails. What is the expected result for new client associations at that branch?
options: The AP automatically converts itself to autonomous mode
The AP stops serving new clients because forwarding depends on the WLC
Clients associate normally and traffic is switched locally by default
Clients are redirected to the service-port interface of the WLC
explain: In local mode a lightweight AP tunnels client traffic to the WLC, so loss of CAPWAP removes the forwarding path for new associations. It does not automatically become autonomous or start local switching; that local-survival behavior describes FlexConnect with local switching.

q: An engineer needs an AP for a warehouse that must make its own RF and security decisions, store its own configuration, and be managed one device at a time. Which choice meets the requirement?
options: A lightweight AP joined to a WLC
An autonomous AP
An AP in sniffer mode
An AP in rogue detector mode
explain: An autonomous AP is self-contained, holding its configuration and making local decisions, at the cost of per-device management. Lightweight APs centralize those decisions on the WLC, and sniffer or rogue detector APs do not serve normal clients.

q: Which two statements describe lightweight APs? (Choose two.)
options: They are configured and managed centrally by a WLC
They communicate with a WLC using CAPWAP tunnels
They store a complete standalone configuration and never need a controller
They can only be managed individually through a local CLI
explain: Lightweight APs join a WLC, receive configuration centrally, and use CAPWAP for control and data. Autonomous APs, not lightweight APs, are the ones managed individually with a complete standalone configuration.

q: A campus refresh replaces dozens of individually configured APs with WLC-managed APs so SSIDs and RF settings can be pushed from one place. What is the primary benefit being sought?
options: Automatic conversion of all ports to routed ports
Centralized configuration and management through the WLC
Elimination of CAPWAP from the design
Each AP will use a different management plane
explain: The lightweight model centralizes WLAN, RF, and policy configuration on the WLC instead of touching every AP. It relies on CAPWAP rather than eliminating it, and it does not change switch ports to routed ports.

q: A packet capture between an AP and a WLC shows UDP traffic destined to port 5246 carrying join and configuration messages. What does this traffic represent?
options: Web authentication traffic to the virtual interface
CAPWAP control traffic
WLC management traffic over HTTPS
CAPWAP data traffic
explain: CAPWAP control traffic uses UDP 5246 and carries discovery, join, configuration, and keepalive messages. CAPWAP data traffic, which tunnels client frames, uses UDP 5247 instead.

q: Client frames tunneled from a local-mode AP to its WLC are seen encapsulated in UDP with destination port 5247. Which CAPWAP channel is being used?
options: The service-port channel
The AP-manager channel
The data channel
The control channel
explain: UDP 5247 is the CAPWAP data port used to tunnel 802.11 client data between AP and WLC in local mode. The control channel on UDP 5246 carries management of the AP itself, not tunneled client frames.

q: An AP is already joined and periodically sends CAPWAP echo requests to its WLC while no user traffic is flowing. On which channel and port do those keepalives travel?
options: Data channel, UDP 5247
Control channel, TCP 5247
Control channel, UDP 5246
Data channel, TCP 5246
explain: Echo requests are CAPWAP control-plane keepalives, carried on UDP 5246. Client data uses UDP 5247, and CAPWAP uses UDP, not TCP, for both channels.

q: In local mode, a wireless client sends a frame to a wired server. How does the lightweight AP handle that frame?
options: It routes it using its own routing table
It encapsulates it in CAPWAP data and sends it to the WLC for forwarding
It bridges it directly onto its local switch port without involving the WLC
It discards it unless FlexConnect local switching is enabled
explain: A local-mode AP tunnels all client traffic in CAPWAP data to the WLC, which then forwards it onto the wired network. Direct local bridging without the WLC describes FlexConnect local switching, not local mode.

q: Which two pairings of CAPWAP traffic type and UDP port are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Data traffic uses TCP 443
Control traffic uses UDP 5247
Control traffic uses UDP 5246
Data traffic uses UDP 5247
explain: CAPWAP control is UDP 5246 and CAPWAP data is UDP 5247. Reversing the ports is incorrect, and neither CAPWAP channel uses TCP 443, which is associated with HTTPS management.

q: A new lightweight AP boots and sends a CAPWAP discovery request before any tunnel is built. What is the purpose of that message?
options: To report a rogue AP on the wired network
To tunnel the first client data frame to a WLC
To find an available WLC and begin the join process
To perform web authentication for a guest user
explain: Discovery is the control-plane step an AP uses to locate candidate WLCs before joining and building its tunnels. It carries no client data, which is only tunneled after the AP has joined.

q: Most APs in a building are left in their default mode: they serve clients on their radios while also performing limited off-channel scanning. Which AP mode is this?
options: Monitor mode
Local mode
Bridge mode
Sniffer mode
explain: Local mode is the default; the AP serves clients and briefly goes off-channel for monitoring tasks. A dedicated monitor-mode AP does not serve clients at all, unlike a local-mode AP.

q: A branch AP is configured for FlexConnect with local switching. The WAN link to the central WLC fails, but previously authenticated branch clients keep passing traffic to local resources. Why?
options: With local switching the AP can forward client traffic locally when disconnected from the WLC
Local mode APs always store a full copy of the WLC configuration
The AP tunnels traffic over the WLC service port instead
FlexConnect APs become autonomous APs permanently after a WAN failure
explain: FlexConnect with local switching lets the AP switch traffic at the branch and survive a WAN outage for local resources. Local mode provides no such survival because traffic is tunneled to the WLC, and the AP does not become a true autonomous AP.

q: An engineer dedicates an AP that never allows client associations and spends all of its time scanning channels for RF and location services. Which mode is configured?
options: Sniffer mode
FlexConnect mode
Monitor mode
Local mode
explain: Monitor mode dedicates the radios to scanning and RF services and does not serve clients. Sniffer mode also does not serve clients, but its job is packet capture forwarded to an analyzer, not continuous channel scanning for RF services.

q: During a troubleshooting session an AP is placed in a mode that captures 802.11 frames and forwards them to a PC running a protocol analyzer. Which mode is this?
options: Monitor mode
Rogue detector mode
Bridge mode
Sniffer mode
explain: Sniffer mode captures wireless frames and sends them to an analyzer such as Wireshark for decoding. Monitor mode scans for RF information but does not stream captured frames to an analyzer in this way.

q: A security team wants an AP connected to a wired trunk that listens for rogue devices appearing on the wired network and helps correlate them, without serving wireless clients. Which mode fits?
options: Bridge mode
Local mode
Rogue detector mode
FlexConnect mode
explain: A rogue detector AP monitors the wired side to detect rogue APs connected to the LAN and does not serve clients. Local and FlexConnect modes are client-serving modes, so they do not match the dedicated wired-detection role.

q: Two buildings without a fiber link must have their wired LANs connected over a wireless link between APs. Which AP mode is designed for this point-to-point use?
options: Rogue detector mode
Sniffer mode
Monitor mode
Bridge mode
explain: Bridge mode, including mesh-style deployments, links remote wired networks together over wireless. Monitor, sniffer, and rogue detector modes are detection or capture roles and do not bridge LANs.

q: Which two statements correctly describe AP modes? (Choose two.)
options: A monitor-mode AP does not serve clients and dedicates its radios to scanning
A FlexConnect AP with local switching can forward traffic locally if the WLC is unreachable
A local-mode AP never needs a WLC to forward client traffic
A sniffer-mode AP serves clients while also routing between LANs
explain: Monitor mode is scanning-only with no client service, and FlexConnect local switching provides local forwarding during WLC loss. Sniffer mode is for packet capture, not client service or routing, and local mode depends on the WLC.

q: An AP in local mode and an AP in FlexConnect local-switching mode both lose contact with the WLC. Which statement correctly compares the outcome?
options: Neither AP retains any radio function under any circumstances
Both continue forwarding all client traffic indefinitely
Only the FlexConnect AP can continue locally switched forwarding; the local-mode AP cannot
Only the local-mode AP continues, because it tunnels traffic
explain: FlexConnect local switching is designed to keep forwarding at the site when the controller is unreachable, while local mode depends on the CAPWAP tunnel to the WLC. Claiming both behave the same ignores the defining difference between the modes.

q: A design note says real-time frame handling stays at the AP while authentication, roaming, and RF management are handled by the WLC. Which concept is being described?
options: FlexConnect local authentication only
Split-MAC architecture
CAPWAP data encapsulation only
Autonomous forwarding
explain: Split-MAC divides the 802.11 MAC functions between the lightweight AP, which handles real-time tasks, and the WLC, which handles management functions. It is broader than encapsulation alone and is the opposite of the fully self-contained autonomous model.

q: Under split-MAC, a client sends a probe request and a beacon is transmitted. Which device primarily handles those real-time functions?
options: The AP, because time-sensitive MAC functions remain at the AP
The DHCP server that offered the AP its address
The switch that powers the AP
The WLC, for every frame including beacons
explain: In split-MAC, time-sensitive functions such as beacons and probe responses stay at the AP, while functions such as authentication policy and roaming are handled at the WLC. Putting every real-time function on the WLC would add unacceptable delay.

q: An administrator browses to a WLC address for in-band management and that same interface is also used by APs on current platforms to reach the controller. Which interface is this?
options: Dynamic interface
Service-port interface
Virtual interface
Management interface
explain: The management interface provides in-band management access and, on modern WLCs, also serves AP join traffic. The virtual interface is not routable for management, and the service port is for out-of-band access only.

q: Guest users redirected for web authentication see a WLC address that is not tied to any physical port and is commonly a nonroutable placeholder address. Which interface are they reaching?
options: Virtual interface
Management interface
A dynamic interface mapped to the guest VLAN
Service-port interface
explain: The virtual interface is a logical, non-physical interface used for functions such as web-auth redirection and DHCP relay identity. It is not a per-WLAN VLAN interface like a dynamic interface, and it is not used for administrator out-of-band access.

q: A technician connects a laptop directly to a dedicated WLC port for out-of-band recovery when the production network is down. Which interface is being used?
options: Virtual interface
Management interface
Dynamic interface
Service-port interface
explain: The service port supports out-of-band management and recovery access isolated from production traffic. It is not used for AP joins or client traffic, which rules out the management and dynamic interfaces for this role.

q: A new WLAN for the engineering department must place its clients into VLAN 30. In the WLC, what must be created and then assigned to that WLAN to make the mapping work?
options: A service-port interface for VLAN 30
A virtual interface for VLAN 30
A dynamic interface mapped to VLAN 30
A second management interface for VLAN 30
explain: Each WLAN is mapped to a dynamic interface, which ties the WLAN to a specific VLAN and subnet on the wired side. The virtual and service-port interfaces have fixed special roles and cannot serve as a per-WLAN VLAN mapping.

q: Documentation for an older WLC refers to a dedicated interface whose sole job was receiving AP join requests, a role now handled by the management interface on newer platforms. Which interface is described?
options: Service-port interface
Virtual interface
Dynamic interface
AP-manager interface
explain: The AP-manager interface historically handled AP-to-WLC join communication before that function was folded into the management interface. Dynamic interfaces map WLANs to VLANs, so they never served as the AP join endpoint.

q: Which two statements about WLC interfaces are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A dynamic interface maps a WLAN to a VLAN
The virtual interface is logical and is used for web-auth redirection
The virtual interface must be assigned to a physical distribution port
The service port carries normal client data traffic
explain: The virtual interface is a logical interface used for redirection and similar functions, and dynamic interfaces bind WLANs to VLANs. The service port is for out-of-band management only, and the virtual interface is not tied to a physical port.

q: The WLC GUI shows Interfaces; Management 10.10.10.10 on Port 1; Virtual 192.0.2.1 with no physical port; Service Port 192.168.1.10 out-of-band; Dynamic Corp-VLAN30 10.30.0.10 on VLAN 30. An auditor asks which address a guest browser is redirected to for web authentication. Which interface supplies it?
options: The virtual interface
The service-port interface
The dynamic Corp-VLAN30 interface
The management interface
explain: Web-auth redirection uses the virtual interface address, shown as 192.0.2.1 with no physical port. The dynamic interface supplies the client subnet and VLAN, not the redirect address, and the service port is for administrators only.

q: All four physical ports on a WLC are cabled to a switch and the administrator wants them to act as one logical link for AP and client traffic. What must be configured on both the WLC and the switch?
options: Spanning tree disabled on the WLC management interface only
DHCP option 43 pointing to each port individually
LAG on the WLC and EtherChannel on the switch ports
A separate dynamic interface on every WLC port
explain: WLC link aggregation bundles the distribution ports into one logical link and requires a matching EtherChannel on the connected switch. Configuring ports individually or adding per-port WLAN interfaces conflicts with how LAG presents the bundle as a single connection.

q: The switch output shows interface Po1; members Gi1/0/1 and Gi1/0/2 bundled; WLC show lag summary shows LAG enabled with two active ports. A third WLC port is cabled but traffic does not use it. What is the most likely cause?
options: The service port has taken over the third port
CAPWAP data uses only two ports by design
The virtual interface is blocking the third port
The third port was added to the switch channel group but LAG bundles must be changed on the WLC side as well and the WLC was not updated
explain: LAG membership must match on both ends; a port added only on the switch will not be used by the WLC bundle until the WLC LAG configuration includes it. CAPWAP has no two-port limit, and neither the virtual nor service-port interface controls bundle membership.

q: A WLC distribution system port connects to a switch to carry traffic for several WLANs that map to different VLANs. How should the switch port normally be configured?
options: As a routed port with an IP address per WLAN
As a trunk carrying the VLANs used by the WLC dynamic interfaces
As an access port in the management VLAN only
As a port with PoE disabled in all cases
explain: Because one WLC connection carries multiple WLAN-to-VLAN mappings, the switch side is normally a trunk for those VLANs (or a LAG trunk when LAG is used). An access port would carry only one VLAN and could not support the other dynamic interfaces.

q: A lightweight AP in a remote subnet receives its IP address by DHCP but never discovers the WLC across the router. The DHCP scope is then updated to include the WLC address. Which mechanism was added?
options: Prior knowledge stored in the AP
DNS resolution of CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER
DHCP option 43
A local broadcast discovery
explain: DHCP option 43 delivers the WLC management address to the AP as part of its DHCP lease, enabling discovery across subnets. A local broadcast would not cross the router, and no DNS name or stored address was mentioned.

q: An AP boots in a branch, has no stored WLC address and no DHCP option 43, but successfully finds the controller after querying a well-known name in its local domain. Which discovery method succeeded?
options: Discovery through the service port
DNS lookup of CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER
Manual configuration of the virtual interface
Broadcast on the local subnet
explain: An AP can resolve CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER in its domain to learn a WLC address when other methods are absent. Broadcast only works on the same subnet and is not what a DNS query describes.

q: A freshly installed AP and a WLC are placed in the same VLAN with no DHCP option 43 and no DNS entry. The AP still discovers the controller. Which method explains this?
options: The AP used the WLC service port by default
The AP used a Layer 3 broadcast discovery on its local subnet
The AP waited for a QoS profile to be assigned
The AP derived the WLC address from its SSID
explain: On the same subnet an AP can find a WLC with a local broadcast discovery request. That method fails across routers, which is why option 43 or DNS is needed in routed designs.

q: After a power outage, an AP rejoins the same WLC it used last month even though DHCP option 43 and DNS are temporarily unavailable. What most likely enabled the join?
options: The AP used web authentication to find the WLC
The AP retained prior knowledge of its previously joined WLC
The monitor-mode radio scanned for the WLC address
The WLC pushed its address through a dynamic interface
