explain: APs remember previously joined controllers and can try those addresses first on reboot. Web auth, monitor mode, and dynamic interfaces are client or WLAN functions and do not supply a stored controller address.

q: A company moves APs to a new routed subnet. The APs get IP addresses but sit in discovery, broadcasts do not reach the data-center WLC, and no DNS record exists. Which single change most directly fixes discovery for all new APs on that subnet?
options: Enable monitor mode on every AP
Change every WLAN to FlexConnect mode
Assign the service port an address on the AP subnet
Add DHCP option 43 with the WLC address to the subnet scope
explain: DHCP option 43 scales to every AP leasing on that subnet and provides the WLC address across a routed boundary. AP mode changes do not supply a controller address, and the service port is not an AP discovery source.

q: Which two methods can a lightweight AP use to learn a WLC address? (Choose two.)
options: DNS resolution of CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER
Reading the address from a WLAN QoS profile
DHCP option 43 supplied in the DHCP offer
Learning it from a client web-auth redirect page
explain: Option 43 and the well-known DNS name are both recognized WLC discovery methods, along with broadcast and prior knowledge. QoS profiles and web-auth pages apply to client traffic on an already-joined AP and never teach an AP its controller.

q: An AP console log shows Discovery request sent; Could not resolve CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER.localdomain; No WLC found; Retrying discovery. No option 43 is configured and the WLC is on another subnet. What does the log indicate?
options: CAPWAP data port 5247 is blocked by a firewall
The DNS discovery method failed and no other cross-subnet method is available
The AP has joined but its QoS profile is missing
The WLAN security tab is misconfigured
explain: The log explicitly shows the DNS name failing to resolve, and with no option 43 and a routed boundary, broadcast cannot reach the WLC either. WLAN and QoS settings are irrelevant because the AP has not yet joined any controller.

q: An administrator must manage a WLC GUI over a network that may be monitored. Which connection should be used?
options: Telnet, because it encrypts CLI management traffic
HTTP with a longer password, because encryption is unnecessary
HTTP, because it is the secure GUI protocol
HTTPS, because it encrypts GUI management traffic
explain: HTTPS provides encrypted web management of the WLC, while HTTP sends GUI traffic in clear text. Telnet is also clear text, and a longer password does not encrypt either insecure protocol.

q: A security audit finds both SSH and Telnet enabled for WLC CLI access. Which action aligns with secure management practice?
options: Use SSH and disable Telnet because SSH encrypts the session
Use Telnet only from the service port to make it secure
Keep Telnet and disable SSH to simplify access
Replace SSH with HTTP for CLI access
explain: SSH encrypts CLI management traffic, whereas Telnet exposes credentials and session content in clear text regardless of which port is used. HTTP is a GUI protocol, not a secure CLI replacement.

q: After hardening, users report the WLC GUI no longer loads on its plain web port but loads normally on the secure web port, and CLI access works only with an encrypted client. What was most likely changed?
options: CAPWAP control was moved from UDP 5246 to TCP 443
All dynamic interfaces were deleted
LAG was enabled on the management interface
HTTP and Telnet were disabled, leaving HTTPS and SSH
explain: Disabling the insecure HTTP and Telnet services leaves HTTPS for the GUI and SSH for the CLI, exactly matching the reported behavior. CAPWAP ports, dynamic interfaces, and LAG do not control which management protocols are offered.

q: In the WLC GUI an administrator selects the WLANs tab, chooses Create New, and enters a profile name and an SSID for a new network. What has been accomplished at this step?
options: The basic WLAN profile has been created and still needs interface and security settings
The AP has been converted to autonomous mode
Web authentication has been enabled for all users
A dynamic interface has been created for the new VLAN
explain: Creating a WLAN from the WLANs tab defines the profile and SSID first; the administrator must still assign an interface, set security, and enable it. No interface, web-auth policy, or AP mode change happens automatically at that step.

q: The WLC GUI shows WLANs > Edit Corp; General tab; Interface set to Corp-VLAN30; Status Enabled; SSID CorpNet. Clients on CorpNet receive addresses from the 10.30.0.0/24 subnet. Why does the interface setting matter?
options: It maps the WLAN to the dynamic interface and VLAN that place clients in that subnet
It sets the virtual interface used for redirection
It selects the CAPWAP port used by the APs
It chooses the QoS profile for voice traffic
explain: Assigning a dynamic interface to a WLAN binds that SSID to a VLAN and subnet, which is why CorpNet clients land in 10.30.0.0/24. CAPWAP ports, QoS profiles, and the virtual interface are configured elsewhere and do not place clients into a VLAN.

q: On a WLAN Security tab an administrator must enable a pre-shared-key network using the mechanics available in this WLC. Which combination should be selected?
options: MAC filtering only with no passphrase
WPA policy disabled and PSK format left blank
Layer 2 security set to None with web policy only
Layer 2 security WPA2 with AES and PSK authentication using the entered passphrase
explain: A PSK WLAN is configured on the Security tab by choosing WPA2 policy with AES encryption and PSK as the key management, then entering the passphrase. Setting Layer 2 security to None provides open access, not a passphrase-protected network.

q: A WLAN was created with the correct SSID, interface, and security, but clients cannot see the SSID at all. In the GUI the WLAN status is unchecked. What is the fix?
options: Move the WLAN to the service-port interface
Change the WLAN to monitor mode
Enable the WLAN status so the WLAN is active and broadcast by its APs
Delete the dynamic interface and recreate it
explain: A newly created WLAN must be enabled before APs advertise it; a disabled status explains a completely invisible SSID. Recreating interfaces or changing AP modes does not activate an otherwise correctly built WLAN.

q: A guest WLAN is intended to let clients associate openly and then present a login page in a browser before granting Internet access. Which WLC setting provides that login-page behavior?
options: FlexConnect local switching on the AP group
Layer 3 web authentication (web policy) on the WLAN
A Platinum QoS profile on the WLAN
A static MAC entry on the access switch
explain: Web authentication is a Layer 3 security feature on the WLAN that redirects a browser to a login page after association. QoS profiles, AP switching modes, and switch MAC entries do not present a web login.

q: Which two steps are part of configuring a basic WLAN in the WLC GUI? (Choose two.)
options: Create the WLAN under the WLANs tab with a profile name and SSID
Set every joined AP to sniffer mode
Assign a dynamic interface so the WLAN maps to the correct VLAN
Configure DHCP option 43 on the WLAN Security tab
explain: Basic WLAN creation happens on the WLANs tab and requires an interface assignment to place clients in a VLAN. Option 43 is a DHCP scope setting for AP discovery, and sniffer mode is an AP role unrelated to WLAN creation.

q: The WLC GUI shows WLANs > Edit Guest; Interface Guest-VLAN40; Security Layer 2 set to None; Security Layer 3 Web Policy checked with Authentication. A guest associates without a passphrase and is then prompted in a browser to log in. Which design is in effect?
options: An open WLAN with Layer 3 web authentication for guests
A monitor-mode WLAN for scanning only
A WPA2/PSK WLAN with a hidden passphrase
A FlexConnect WLAN with local authentication only
explain: Layer 2 None means open association with no passphrase, and the checked Layer 3 web policy provides the browser login, which is the classic guest web-auth design. It is not a PSK network, and AP modes do not define this WLAN security combination.

q: Two WLANs exist on one WLC: one reuses the same profile name pattern for staff and one for visitors, but users complain a phone joins the visitor SSID when they tap the staff name they see. What GUI concept explains that users connect by SSID, not by the internal label?
options: The profile name is only an internal WLC label; the SSID is the network name clients see and join
The WLAN ID is the name broadcast in beacons
Clients join by dynamic interface name
The SSID is stored only on the virtual interface
explain: The WLC profile name identifies the WLAN inside the controller, while the SSID is the broadcast name a client selects. Clients never see dynamic interface names or WLAN IDs as the network name in a scan list.

q: A voice handset WLAN needs the highest-priority QoS treatment available as a WLAN profile on the WLC. Which profile should be applied?
options: Bronze
Platinum
Gold
Silver
explain: In WLC QoS profiles, Platinum is intended for voice-grade priority, above Gold for video and Silver for best-effort enterprise traffic. Bronze is background-level and would be the worst choice for voice.

q: A WLAN carrying mainly bulk background transfers should not compete with interactive traffic. Which WLC QoS profile best matches that intent at awareness level?
options: Platinum
Silver with voice priority
Gold
Bronze
explain: Bronze provides background or lowest-priority handling suitable for bulk traffic that should yield to other applications. Platinum and Gold reserve higher priority for voice and video and would defeat the stated intent.

q: An administrator opens a WLAN in the GUI and finds a QoS tab listing Platinum, Gold, Silver, and Bronze. What is the effect of choosing one for this WLAN?
options: It enables web authentication for that WLAN
It changes the CAPWAP data port for that WLAN
It sets the QoS profile applied to traffic on that WLAN
It assigns the WLAN to a new dynamic interface
explain: The QoS tab selection applies a per-WLAN QoS profile that influences how that WLAN traffic is prioritized. It does not alter CAPWAP ports, VLAN assignment, or Layer 3 web-auth settings, which live on other tabs.

q: A ceiling AP has a single Ethernet cable run to a PoE switch port and no local power adapter, yet it powers on and passes data. How is this possible?
options: Power over Ethernet delivers both power and data over the same cable from the switch
The AP harvests power from its radios
The WLC sends power over the CAPWAP tunnel
The service port supplies power to all APs
explain: PoE lets the access switch supply electrical power and Ethernet data over one cable to the AP, which is the standard physical installation method. CAPWAP is a logical tunnel and carries no electrical power.

q: After a switch upgrade, several APs on one switch reboot intermittently and some radios stay disabled while wired devices on the same switch work normally. Which physical-layer cause should be checked first?
options: DNS resolution of CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER
The WLC virtual interface address
The WLAN QoS profile assigned to the SSIDs
Insufficient PoE power budget on the switch for all attached APs
explain: APs that reboot or disable radios under load commonly indicate the switch cannot deliver enough PoE power to all ports within its budget. Virtual interfaces, QoS profiles, and DNS do not supply electrical power.

q: A WLC must carry traffic for WLANs mapped to VLANs 10, 20, and 30 back to the campus core. Which physical connection design supports all three?
options: One access link in VLAN 10 only
A trunk (or LAG trunk) to the switch carrying VLANs 10, 20, and 30
Three separate service-port connections, one per VLAN
A console connection to the core switch
explain: A trunk or aggregated trunk from the WLC distribution ports carries every VLAN used by its dynamic interfaces. A single access link would carry only one VLAN, and the service and console ports are for management, not client data.

q: A PC connects to switch port Gi1/0/5 in VLAN 10 and sends its first frame. How does the switch populate its MAC address table from that frame?
options: It floods the frame and learns nothing
It learns the destination MAC and maps it to Gi1/0/5
It learns the source MAC and maps it to Gi1/0/5 in VLAN 10
It creates a static entry that will never age out
explain: Switches learn from the source MAC address of incoming frames and record the ingress port and VLAN. Learning the destination would be useless because the frame arrived from the source, and learned entries are dynamic, not static.

q: A server that must always be reachable on the same switch port has its MAC address manually configured in the table. How does that entry differ from a learned entry?
options: A static entry is removed after 30 seconds of inactivity
A static entry can only exist in VLAN 1
A static entry is learned from the destination address of frames
A static entry does not age out and remains until removed by configuration
explain: Manually configured static MAC entries are persistent and do not age, unlike dynamic entries that expire after inactivity. They are entered by an administrator, not learned from frame destinations.

q: A dynamic MAC entry for a laptop that was unplugged last week is no longer present when an engineer checks the table today, and no one cleared it manually. What explains its absence?
options: Broadcast frames delete the oldest entry each hour
Static entries overwrite all dynamic entries at midnight
The switch converts unused dynamic entries to routed entries
Dynamic entries age out after a period without frames from that source
explain: Dynamic entries are removed by the aging process when no traffic from that MAC is seen for the aging period. No manual clear is needed, and the other choices describe mechanisms that do not exist in normal switch operation.

q: The output shows show mac address-table; VLAN 10; Address 0a1b.2c3d.4e5f; Type DYNAMIC; Port Gi1/0/5; VLAN 10; Address 0a1b.9a9a.1111; Type STATIC; Port Gi1/0/8. A frame in VLAN 10 arrives destined for 0a1b.2c3d.4e5f. Out which port will the switch forward it?
options: No port, because dynamic entries are only for learning
Gi1/0/8, because static entries take precedence for all destinations
Gi1/0/5, because that is the port recorded for that destination MAC
All VLAN 10 ports, because the entry is dynamic
explain: The table maps that destination to Gi1/0/5, so the switch forwards the known unicast out that single port. The static entry belongs to a different MAC address and does not redirect traffic for this destination.

q: Which two statements about switch MAC address tables are correct? (Choose two.)
options: All entries are permanent once any frame is received
Dynamic entries are learned from destination MAC addresses
Dynamic entries are learned from source MAC addresses and age out
Static entries are configured manually and do not age out
explain: Switches learn dynamic entries from source addresses and remove them through aging, while static entries are manual and persistent. Destination addresses are used for lookup, not learning, and learned entries are not permanent.

q: A laptop moves from port Gi1/0/2 to Gi1/0/9 in the same VLAN and sends traffic. A coworker still sees reachability without manual table changes. Why?
options: The switch floods all traffic for that MAC forever after a move
The switch updates the dynamic entry to Gi1/0/9 when frames arrive with that source MAC on the new port
The old entry must always be cleared by an administrator before any move works
Static entries automatically follow the laptop
explain: When frames from the same source MAC arrive on a new port, the switch updates its dynamic entry to the new location. Manual clearing can speed convergence in odd cases but is not required for normal learning to update the entry.

q: A switch has a MAC table entry showing a server in VLAN 20 reachable via Gi1/0/12. A unicast frame for that server arrives on another port. What does the switch do?
options: Forwards it only out Gi1/0/12 and filters it from other ports
Floods it to all VLAN 20 ports to be safe
Sends it to the WLC for a forwarding decision
Drops it because the ingress port is not Gi1/0/12
explain: A known unicast is forwarded only out the recorded port, which simultaneously filters it from all other ports. Flooding is reserved for unknown destinations, broadcasts, and multicast without snooping constraints.

q: A host in VLAN 15 sends a frame to a MAC address that is not in the switch MAC table. What forwarding action does the switch take?
options: It drops the frame and sends an error to the source
It floods the frame out all ports in VLAN 15 except the ingress port
It stores it until the destination is learned by ARP alone
It forwards it only to the default gateway port
explain: An unknown unicast is flooded within its VLAN, excluding the port it arrived on, so the destination can receive it and reply. Dropping it would break communication with hosts the switch has simply not learned yet.

q: A frame arrives on Gi1/0/3 addressed to a broadcast destination in VLAN 10. How does the switch handle it?
options: It sends it only to ports with input errors
It forwards it only out the port with a static entry
It filters it because broadcasts are never forwarded
It floods it out all active ports in VLAN 10 except Gi1/0/3
explain: Broadcast frames are flooded to every port in the same VLAN except the ingress port so all hosts in the broadcast domain receive them. They are not limited to a single learned or static port.

q: A frame arrives on Gi1/0/4 and its destination MAC is already learned as being on Gi1/0/4 itself, as with two virtual hosts behind the same port segment. What does the switch do?
options: It forwards it to the WLC by default
It floods the frame to the whole VLAN
It filters the frame and does not forward it back out Gi1/0/4 or to other ports
It creates a static entry and then floods it
explain: When source and destination are on the same port, the switch filters the frame because the destination can already receive it locally without switch forwarding. Flooding would waste bandwidth and is used only for unknown or broadcast destinations.

q: Which two forwarding behaviors are correct for a Layer 2 switch? (Choose two.)
options: A broadcast frame is forwarded out only the single best port
A frame whose destination is on the same port as its source is filtered
A known unicast is flooded to every port in the VLAN
An unknown unicast is flooded within its VLAN except on the ingress port
explain: Unknown unicasts are flooded in the VLAN and same-port destinations are filtered, both to deliver traffic without unnecessary copies. Known unicasts go to one port only, and broadcasts go to all VLAN ports except the ingress port.

q: The output shows show mac address-table; VLAN 20; Host A learned on Gi1/0/1; Host B learned on Gi1/0/2; no entry for Host C. Host A sends one frame to Host B and then one frame to Host C. How do the two forwarding decisions differ?
options: The frame to Host B goes only out Gi1/0/2, while the frame to Host C is flooded to all VLAN 20 ports except Gi1/0/1
Both frames are flooded because Host C is unknown
The frame to Host B is flooded and the frame to Host C is dropped
Both frames are forwarded only out Gi1/0/2
explain: Host B is a known unicast, so its frame is forwarded to Gi1/0/2 only; Host C is unknown, so its frame is flooded within VLAN 20 except the ingress port. Treating both the same ignores whether a table entry exists for the destination.

q: An access port reports many runts in its interface counters while users on that port report corrupted transfers. What does a runt indicate?
options: A frame dropped by storm control for exceeding a broadcast threshold
A frame with a correct size but a wrong VLAN tag
A frame smaller than the minimum 64-byte Ethernet frame, often from a collision or faulty NIC
A frame larger than the maximum permitted size
explain: Runts are undersized frames below the 64-byte Ethernet minimum, typically caused by collisions or a bad transmitter. Oversized frames are giants, which is the opposite condition.

q: The output shows show interfaces Gi1/0/7; 842 input errors; 790 CRC; 15 runts; 22 giants; users report intermittent loss on that access port. Which conclusion is best supported by the counters?
options: The port is experiencing physical-layer or duplex-related errors that corrupt frames and should be checked at the cabling and NIC level
Storm control is working correctly and no action is needed
The WLAN QoS profile on the switch is set to Bronze
The MAC table has aged out too quickly
explain: Rising input errors with CRC failures plus runts and giants point to frames being damaged or malformed on that link, a Layer 1 or duplex problem, not a table-aging or QoS issue. Storm control counters would describe dropped excess traffic, not CRC corruption.

q: A floor switch port connected to an AP is overwhelmed when a faulty device floods broadcast traffic, degrading the whole VLAN. Which feature can limit this type of traffic on the port?
options: DHCP option 43
Storm control
MAC aging
Split-MAC
explain: Storm control monitors broadcast, multicast, or unicast traffic levels on a port and drops excess traffic or shuts the port when a threshold is exceeded. The other features deal with address learning, wireless architecture, or AP discovery.

q: Storm control is set on an access port with an action to shut the port down when broadcast traffic exceeds its threshold, and a loop later triggers that threshold. What happens to the port?
options: It converts itself to a trunk port
It ages out all MAC entries in the VLAN
It keeps forwarding but logs a warning only
It is placed into an err-disabled state when the threshold is exceeded, stopping the storm
explain: With a shutdown action configured, exceeding the storm-control threshold err-disables the port, which stops the offending traffic at the source. A trap-only or drop configuration would behave differently, but the stated action is shutdown.

q: Four access switches in a wiring closet are cabled together so they are managed as one unit with a single configuration and appear as one switch to the rest of the network. Which technology provides this at awareness level?
options: FlexConnect, where APs form one logical controller
Storm control, where ports share one threshold
Switch stacking, where members form one logical switch
LAG on a WLC, where ports form one AP
explain: Stacking technologies such as StackWise combine multiple physical switches into a single logical switch with unified management. FlexConnect, WLC LAG, and storm control operate on APs, controller ports, and traffic thresholds, not on unifying switch management.

q: In a switch stack, one member loses its power supply but its ports stay up because power is drawn from other members in the stack. Which companion technology is providing this?
options: CAPWAP control channel redundancy
StackPower, which shares power among stack members
MAC table synchronization
PoE negotiation with the WLC
explain: StackPower allows stack members to pool and share power supplies so a member can survive the loss of its own supply. It is distinct from data stacking, and none of the other options supply electrical power between switches.

q: Which command shows the administrative distance and metric of installed routes?
