show ip interface brief
q: Which command displays the gateway of last resort and the routing table codes legend on R28?

explain: For the identical /16, static AD 1 beats eBGP AD 20, so only the static is installed in the RIB; the BGP path remains in the BGP table. Two different-AD routes to one prefix do not both install for per-packet choice.
options: The BGP route because eBGP is an external protocol
Only the static route; the BGP entry shown came from the BGP table, not a second installed path
Only the BGP route, and the static is shown for reference
Both routes are installed and the router chooses per packet
q: Look at this output on R10: Codes: C - connected, S - static, B - BGP; B 10.88.0.0/16 [20/0] via 203.0.113.2, 01:02:03; S 10.88.0.0/16 [1/0] via 192.168.10.2; C 192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0. Which route is actually installed for forwarding?

explain: Over-summarization makes R29 claim networks it cannot reach, black-holing traffic for .0/24 and .3/24. Statics install regardless of component routes, and classful boundaries do not block a /22 summary.
options: The static route will fail to install without all component routes present
Traffic for the missing /24s is attracted to R29 and dropped or misforwarded — over-summarization
The hub will reject the summary because it is not a classful boundary
No problem, because summary routes only attract matching traffic they can deliver
q: Summary route risk: R29 advertises a static summary 172.16.0.0/22 toward a hub, but only 172.16.1.0/24 and 172.16.2.0/24 exist locally; 172.16.0.0/24 and 172.16.3.0/24 belong elsewhere. What problem can occur?

explain: Raising the static's AD above the primary protocol keeps it floating, and IOS automatically removes it from the table again when the lower-AD primary returns. AD 0 is reserved behavior for connected routes and dual masks create different prefixes, not a backup.
options: Set the static route's AD to 0 so it ties with connected routes
Set the static route's AD higher than the dynamic protocol's AD
Configure the same static route twice with different masks
Configure the static route and rely on it being withdrawn when the primary returns
q: Which two actions are valid ways to make a backup static route appear only after a primary dynamic route fails? (Choose two.)

explain: On each Ethernet hop the frame is addressed to the next hop's MAC, which the router resolves via ARP for the next-hop IP. ARP for the final destination only happens when the destination is on a directly connected network.
options: The MAC address of the gateway of last resort in all cases
The MAC address corresponding to the next-hop IP address
The MAC address of the final destination host
No ARP is needed because routers forward using IP only
q: R30's forwarding process for a packet via a next-hop route includes resolving the Layer 2 address. Which address does R30 ARP for on the outgoing Ethernet link?

explain: The AD is appended as a plain number at the end of the ip route command, after the next hop. There is no distance keyword in this syntax, and the value does not lead the command.
q: Retail router R31 needs a static route to HQ network 10.31.0.0/16 via 192.168.31.2 with an AD of 130 to serve as backup to RIP (120). Which command is correct?

explain: The configured next hop 192.168.99.2 does not match the actual peer 192.168.32.2, and R32 has no path to 192.168.99.0, so recursion fails. Correcting the next hop, not widening the destination mask, fixes the route.
options: Static routes cannot be used on WAN interfaces at branch sites
The route needs the permanent keyword to survive interface changes
The next hop 192.168.99.2 is in a network R32 has no route to reach
The destination mask should be 255.255.0.0 for a branch network
q: Branch R32 was configured with ip route 10.32.0.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.99.2, but the WAN interface is 192.168.32.1/24 and the peer is 192.168.32.2. Users cannot reach 10.32.0.0/24. What is the fault?

explain: Bracket format is always [AD/metric], so 90 is EIGRP internal AD and 2176 is the composite metric. Reading the first value as the metric is the classic output-interpretation error.
options: It is correct because the first number is always the metric
It is wrong: 2176 is the AD and 90 is the hop count
It is correct because EIGRP does not use administrative distance
It is wrong: 90 is the AD and 2176 is the EIGRP metric
q: On R33, show ip route displays D 10.33.0.0/16 [90/2176]. An engineer claims the metric is 90. How should this claim be evaluated?

explain: 172.16.9.200 lies in the connected 172.16.9.128/25 (.128-.255), the longest match among /16, /24, and /25. Longest prefix wins before AD, so the connected route forwards it locally.
options: The connected /25 route on GigabitEthernet0/2
The OSPF /24 route via 10.34.0.6
The static /16 route via 10.34.0.2
The packet loops between the static and OSPF next hops
q: Clinic router R34 has routes: S 172.16.0.0/16 [1/0] via 10.34.0.2; O 172.16.9.0/24 [110/45] via 10.34.0.6; C 172.16.9.128/25 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2. A packet for 172.16.9.200 arrives. Which route is used?

explain: Working statics are verified in the routing table itself and by confirming traffic for a test destination follows the intended match. Interface brief shows interfaces, not routes, and only a default static affects the gateway of last resort.
options: A more specific test destination is checked against the expected longest match
The route appears in show ip route with the expected S code and next hop
The route appears in show ip interface brief with status up/up
The gateway of last resort always changes to the new next hop
q: Which two verifications confirm a newly configured static route is working at the routing-table level? (Choose two.)

explain: AD ties for an identical prefix are not a design tool; the incumbent route is generally retained and behavior should not be relied upon. Intent must be expressed with an unambiguous AD — lower to prefer the static, higher to float it.
options: With truly equal AD for the identical prefix, the first installed route is retained; an engineer should not rely on a tie and should set a clearly higher or lower AD
The static wins because statics always beat RIP regardless of AD
RIP wins because dynamic protocols preempt statics at equal AD
Both routes install and cause a routing loop by design
q: A route to 10.36.0.0/16 is offered by RIP at AD 120 and by a static configured with distance 120 for the same prefix and equal conditions claimed by two engineers. What determines the outcome and what is the safe exam conclusion?

explain: Identical prefix and length means AD decides, and static AD 1 beats OSPF 110. Uptime and the presence of an interface name in the OSPF line do not affect source selection.
options: The static route because its AD 1 is lower than OSPF's 110 for the identical /24
The OSPF route because it lists an exit interface explicitly
The OSPF route because its uptime of 00:31:00 is longer
Traffic alternates because the next hops share one connected subnet
q: Examine the output on R12: Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF; O 10.37.0.0/24 [110/20] via 192.168.12.2, 00:31:00, GigabitEthernet0/0; S 10.37.0.0/24 [1/0] via 192.168.12.6; C 192.168.12.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0. Both entries appear in a debug capture history. Which one forwards traffic now?

explain: Four /24s aligned at .16 summarize to a /22, mask 255.255.252.0, covering .16 through .19. A /21 (255.255.248.0) would also swallow .20-.23, and /23 covers only two networks.
q: Hotel network router R36 summarizes branch LANs 192.168.16.0/24, 192.168.17.0/24, 192.168.18.0/24, and 192.168.19.0/24. Which summary mask is correct?

explain: A static whose exit path is down is removed from the table, so no default remains and unmatched Internet traffic is dropped. Connected routes are never promoted to a default role.
options: The default route is withdrawn and traffic is dropped for lack of a match
The router promotes the best connected route to gateway of last resort
Traffic uses the default because static routes ignore interface state
Traffic is redirected to the connected network with the lowest address
q: R37's only routes are connected networks and one static default via 203.0.113.1, but the interface toward 203.0.113.1 is administratively shut down. What is the forwarding result for Internet destinations?

explain: AD 100 exceeds EIGRP internal's 90, so the static floats as a backup. AD 80 or 1 would immediately displace EIGRP, and exactly 90 creates an unreliable tie instead of a clean backup.
q: R38 needs a backup path to 10.38.0.0/16 currently learned by EIGRP internal (90). Which floating static configuration is valid?

explain: The no form must specify the same network, mask, and next hop (or interface) as the existing route; a mismatched next hop removes nothing. This is a frequent cause of stale statics surviving a change.
options: Nothing is removed because the no form must match the original route's parameters
IOS returns the route to its default AD of 110 instead
Both next-hop versions are removed from the configuration
The original route is removed because the prefix matches
q: During a change window, an engineer removes a static route with no ip route 10.39.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.168.39.2 but mistypes the next hop as 192.168.39.9. What happens?

explain: Each router decrements TTL by one before forwarding; a packet arriving with TTL 1 cannot be forwarded without expiring, so it is dropped and ICMP Time Exceeded is sent. TTL is never reset mid-path by a transit router.
options: The router resets the TTL to 64 and forwards it on the WAN link
The router holds it until the destination sends a TTL refresh
The router forwards it anyway because TTL applies only to the source host
The router drops it instead of forwarding, because forwarding would reduce the TTL to 0
q: Factory router R39 forwards a packet and decrements the TTL. At which point in handling does the TTL reach zero and cause a drop with an ICMP Time Exceeded, assuming the incoming TTL was 1?

explain: For identical prefixes, AD outranks metric reasoning across protocols: static AD 1 beats EIGRP AD 90. A static metric of 0 is normal, and alphabetical code order has no role in selection.
options: The trainee is right; a metric of 0 means the static is a placeholder
The trainee is wrong; AD is compared first across sources, so the static at AD 1 forwards
Both forward alternately because the prefixes are identical
EIGRP forwards because D routes install before S routes alphabetically
q: Examine this output on R14: Codes: C - connected, S - static, D - EIGRP; D 10.60.0.0/16 [90/3072] via 10.0.14.2, 00:04:18, GigabitEthernet0/1; S 10.60.0.0/16 [1/0] via 10.0.14.6; C 10.0.14.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1. A trainee says EIGRP forwards because its metric is meaningful while the static metric is 0. What is the correct assessment?

explain: 255.255.240.0 is a /20, covering 16 /24s from 172.16.0.0 to 172.16.15.255. It is a summary covering all sixteen networks, not just the base network or a /22-sized block of four.
options: Only the single network 172.16.0.0 with mask /20
q: School router R40 is configured with ip route 172.16.0.0 255.255.240.0 10.40.0.2. Which set of networks does this single static cover?

explain: AD 20 identifies eBGP as the source, and the via field gives next hop 203.0.113.2. The 20 is not an AS count, and eBGP by definition comes from a different AS, so local origin is false.
options: The next hop for the prefix is 203.0.113.2
The prefix originated inside the local autonomous system
The route was learned via eBGP, indicated by AD 20
The path contains exactly 20 autonomous systems
q: Which two facts can be determined directly from the line B 10.70.0.0/16 [20/0] via 203.0.113.2 in a routing table? (Choose two.)

explain: A static whose next hop is only reachable via the default route creates circular recursion and unpredictable forwarding. Sound design points statics at next hops on directly connected networks.
options: The static becomes a host route automatically to avoid the loop
No flaw; resolving statics through the default is the recommended design
A recursive loop through the default route; the static may install unstably or forward traffic back toward the default path unexpectedly
The default route's AD rises to 255 to protect the static route
q: ISP edge router R42 receives a packet for a destination matched by a static route whose next hop resolves through the default route itself. What design flaw does this reveal, and what is the likely result?

explain: The /16 RIP route is more specific than /0, so longest-prefix match sends the packet to 10.0.15.2. The gateway of last resort is only for destinations with no more specific match, regardless of RIP's AD.
options: 198.51.100.1, because RIP's AD of 120 makes its route untrusted
198.51.100.1, because the gateway of last resort handles all routed traffic
10.0.15.2, because the RIP /16 is a longer match than the default /0
10.0.15.2 only after the default route times out
q: Consider the output on R15: Codes: C - connected, S - static, R - RIP; Gateway of last resort is 198.51.100.1 to network 0.0.0.0; S* 0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 198.51.100.1; R 10.95.0.0/16 [120/4] via 10.0.15.2, 00:00:09, Serial0/0/0. A packet for 10.95.3.3 arrives. Which next hop is used and why?

explain: After the static is removed, AD again decides between different protocols: EIGRP 90 beats OSPF 110. Comparing EIGRP's 5000 metric against OSPF's 20 across protocols is invalid.
options: OSPF, because its metric of 20 is the lowest remaining
Both, because the tie in prefix length forces load sharing
EIGRP, because AD 90 is lower than OSPF's 110 once the static is gone
Neither, because deleting a static disables dynamic backup
q: An engineer compares candidate routes for 10.96.0.0/24: static AD 1 metric 0, OSPF AD 110 metric 20, EIGRP AD 90 metric 5000. If the static is deleted, which route installs next?

explain: Only the routing table proves activation: the gateway line plus the S* entry confirm the default is installed. The running-config merely proves the command was typed, even if the next hop is unreachable and the route never installed.
options: show ip interface brief shows the WAN interface protocol is up
show ip route shows Gateway of last resort is set to the static's next hop with an S* entry
show ip protocols shows static listed as a routing protocol
show running-config shows the ip route 0.0.0.0 command in the configuration
q: Which command and result best verify that R44's default static route is the active gateway of last resort?

explain: Metrics are never compared between different protocols, so equal AD gives no clean metric-based override. The professional fix is to give the static an unambiguously lower AD to prefer it or higher to float it.
options: The static is rejected by IOS because its AD equals a dynamic protocol
AD ties at 110, and cross-protocol metric comparison does not occur, so the result is not the deterministic override the engineer expected; a distinct AD should be used
The static wins because metric 0 is lower than 31 across protocols
OSPF is uninstalled and a loop forms between the two entries
q: R45 has an OSPF route to 10.45.0.0/24 [110/31] and later an engineer adds a static to the same /24 with AD 110 and metric 0, expecting the static to win on metric. What actually happens and why?

explain: IS-IS AD 115 beats RIP AD 120 for the identical prefix. Protocol family does not confer trust, and metrics are not compared across protocols.
options: RIP wins: its AD 120 counts hops more accurately
IS-IS wins: its AD 115 is lower than RIP's 120
Neither wins until metrics are compared across both protocols
RIP wins because distance-vector protocols are trusted over link-state
q: Two engineers debate AD for IS-IS versus RIP on R47 for the same prefix. One says IS-IS wins, the other says RIP wins because it is distance-vector like EIGRP. Who is right?

explain: Floating behavior needs a higher AD than OSPF (for example 120) and a healthy primary OSPF route for the identical prefix to keep the static withdrawn. Re-adding order does not matter, and lengthening the mask creates a different prefix that would win by longest match instead.
options: Change the static route's destination mask to a longer prefix
Ensure the OSPF route to the identical prefix is present and healthy so the higher-AD static stays out of the table
Remove the static and re-add it so it is learned after OSPF
Reconfigure the static with an AD of 120, above OSPF's 110
q: Which two changes would convert a working primary static route into a floating backup for an OSPF route to the same prefix? (Choose two.)

explain: Route installation depends on next-hop reachability at evaluation time; once the connected route existed, recursion succeeded, the default installed, and the gateway was set. IOS does not delay the gateway line or require a manual clear for a newly valid static.
options: The gateway line updates only once per hour in IOS output
Static defaults require a manual clear ip route before first use
The default static could not install until its next hop became reachable through the connected route
The ping test itself installed the gateway of last resort
q: On R48, a static default is configured but show ip route reports Gateway of last resort is not set. The WAN interface shows up/up in show ip interface brief and the next hop pings successfully via a connected route installed later. After the connected route appeared, the engineer rechecks and the gateway is now set. What best explains the earlier state?

explain: Prefix length is per-destination: .130 matches both /24 and /25 and takes the longer /25, while .10 matches only the /24. A /24 is routinely subdivided by more specific routes.
options: No, all hosts in a /24 must always follow the same route
Yes, the /25 static is a longer match for .130, while .10 only matches the /24
Yes, because the static route's AD forces all /24 traffic to split
No, static routes cannot be more specific than a /24
q: R49 forwards packets for 192.168.70.0/24 via OSPF and for 192.168.70.128/25 via a static route. A host at 192.168.70.130 reports a different path than a host at 192.168.70.10. Is this expected?

explain: Ranking is eBGP 20 first, OSPF 110 second, so a tertiary static needs AD above 110 to stay behind both. Exceeding only 20 would still place it ahead of OSPF if set between 21 and 110, and AD 1 would make it primary.
options: It must exceed 20, the eBGP administrative distance
It must be set to 1 so it is evaluated last by the router
It must equal 115 to rank with IS-IS in the table
It must exceed 110, the OSPF administrative distance, so it ranks behind both dynamic routes
q: Senior engineer review: a proposed design installs, for prefix 10.110.0.0/16, an eBGP route as primary and a floating static as tertiary backup behind an OSPF route. What AD must the static exceed to truly be tertiary?

explain: An exit-interface static depends on that interface being up; down/down withdraws it from the RIB. The /16 mask is valid, interface-only statics are legitimate, and a missing gateway does not hide specific routes.
options: The mask 255.255.0.0 is invalid for a static route command
The route is hidden because no gateway of last resort exists
Static routes require a next-hop address and never an interface
The static uses an exit interface that is down, so the route is not installed
q: Troubleshoot R50: show ip route lacks the 10.120.0.0/16 static, show running-config contains ip route 10.120.0.0 255.255.0.0 GigabitEthernet0/3, and show ip interface brief shows GigabitEthernet0/3 as down/down. What is the root cause?

explain: OSPF AD 110 is lower than the static's configured 115, so OSPF forwards and the static floats as intended. Configured AD on a static is honored, not ignored, and E2 denotes an OSPF external type 2 route needing no activation.
options: Neither forwards because E2 routes require a static backup to activate
The static forwards because statics ignore configured AD values
The OSPF route forwards; the static at AD 115 correctly floats behind OSPF's 110
The static forwards; its AD 115 was set to float it, but 115 still beats OSPF here
q: Look at this output on R17: Codes: C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF; O E2 10.130.0.0/24 [110/20] via 172.16.17.2, 00:02:41, GigabitEthernet0/0; S 10.130.0.0/24 [115/0] via 172.16.17.6. Which route forwards traffic and what is notable about the static?

explain: Forwarding uses the RIB, not the configuration: an installed S entry with resolvable next hop proves the route will be used. A configured-but-uninstalled static (for example with an unreachable next hop) forwards nothing.
options: Confirming the static route's AD is set to the default value of 1
Confirming the route is installed in show ip route with a reachable next hop or up exit interface
Confirming the router hostname matches the design document
Confirming the command exists under show running-config
q: Which final verification step distinguishes a router that merely has a static route configured from one that will actually forward with it?

explain: Down means no hellos have been received from the neighbor, which matches a silent link. Init requires a hello received from the neighbor that does not yet list this router, so it cannot apply when nothing was received.
options: Two-Way
Down
Init
Full
q: A router sends OSPF hello packets on a new interface but receives no hellos back from any neighbor on that link. In which neighbor state will an entry for a potential neighbor remain if no hello is ever received?

explain: Init means a hello was received but this router's ID was absent from it, so one-way visibility exists. Two-Way is only reached once each router sees its own ID in the other's hello.
options: R2 has seen R1 and bidirectional communication is established
The LSDBs are synchronized and the state is Full
The routers are exchanging database descriptors in ExStart
R1 has seen R2 but bidirectional communication is not yet confirmed, so the state is Init
q: Router R1 receives a hello from R2, but the hello does not contain R1's router ID in its neighbor list. What does this tell R1 about the neighbor relationship with R2?

explain: On broadcast networks DROTHERs stop at Two-Way with each other to reduce adjacency overhead, going Full only with the DR and BDR. Expecting Full between DROTHERs misreads a healthy design as a fault.
options: It is normal only on point-to-point links, never on broadcast links
It is normal; DROTHERs stay at Two-Way with each other and go Full only with the DR and BDR
It is a fault; DROTHERs must reach Full with each other
It is a fault; they should be in Loading until the DR fails
q: On a broadcast Ethernet segment with a DR and BDR elected, two DROTHER routers reach the Two-Way state with each other and stop there. An engineer claims this is a fault. What is the correct assessment?

explain: ExStart is where master/slave negotiation and the initial DBD sequence number are agreed. Exchange comes afterward, when the actual DBD packets describing LSDB contents are sent.
options: ExStart
Init
Loading
Exchange
q: Two OSPF routers have reached Two-Way and are now negotiating which router will initiate the database description exchange and with what initial sequence number. Which state are they in?

explain: Loading is when link-state requests are sent and the missing LSAs are awaited via updates. In Exchange the routers only trade DBD summaries, not the requested full LSAs.
options: ExStart
Exchange
Full
Loading
q: During adjacency formation, R1 has received DBD summaries from R2 and finds it is missing three LSAs, so it sends link-state requests for them and waits for updates. Which state best describes R1 at this moment?

explain: Full means the adjacency is complete and the LSDBs are synchronized, so SPF can be run on identical data. Hello exchange alone only proves Two-Way, not synchronization.
options: Their LSDBs for the area are synchronized and they can forward using routes built from that database
One of them is necessarily the DR for the segment
They have agreed on a router ID for the segment
They have exchanged hellos but not LSAs
q: An engineer verifies an OSPF adjacency and sees the neighbor listed as Full. What does Full guarantee about the two routers?

explain: An interface MTU mismatch is the classic cause of ExStart/Exchange looping because DBDs carrying the larger MTU are rejected. Different OSPF process IDs are locally significant only and never block adjacency.
options: An MTU mismatch causing DBD packets to be rejected
A passive interface on one side
Different OSPF process IDs
Duplicate router IDs
q: Two routers connected by Ethernet are stuck in ExStart/Exchange and repeatedly retransmit DBDs. Both interfaces are up and timers match, but one interface has an MTU of 1500 and the other is set to 9000. What is the most likely cause?

explain: With simultaneous boot, the highest OSPF interface priority wins the DR election, so priority 100 is elected. Router ID is only the tie-breaker when priorities are equal.
options: The router with priority 1
The router with priority 100
The router with priority 50
The router with priority 10
q: Four routers on a broadcast segment have OSPF priorities of 1, 10, 50, and 100, and all boot at the same time. Which router becomes the DR?

explain: When priorities tie, the highest router ID wins, so 10.1.1.9 becomes DR. The lowest router ID does not win; that reverses the tie-break rule.
options: 10.1.1.1, because the lowest router ID wins ties
10.1.1.9, because the highest router ID wins ties
10.1.1.5, because the middle router ID wins ties
None, because equal priorities prevent any election
q: Three routers on a segment all have the default OSPF priority of 1. Their router IDs are 10.1.1.1, 10.1.1.9, and 10.1.1.5. If they boot together, which becomes DR and why?

explain: OSPF DR election is non-preemptive, so a later-joining higher-priority router becomes at most BDR and waits. It does not displace a stable DR despite its higher priority.
options: The segment holds a new election and the BDR becomes DR
Both routers share the DR role until the next hello interval
The new router immediately takes over as DR because its priority is higher
The existing DR remains DR because DR election is non-preemptive
q: A segment already has a working DR with priority 50. A new router with priority 200 is connected and boots. What happens to the DR role?

explain: When the DR fails, the BDR is promoted to DR and only the vacant BDR role is filled by election. A full re-election of both roles does not occur.
options: The segment operates without a DR until all routers reload
The BDR is promoted to DR and a new BDR is elected from the DROTHERs
A completely new election is held among all DROTHERs for both roles
The DROTHER with the lowest router ID becomes DR
q: The DR for a broadcast segment fails. No other failure occurs. What happens next on that segment?

explain: Priority 0 makes a router ineligible for DR/BDR election while still allowing normal DROTHER adjacencies. It does not block adjacency formation entirely.
options: It cannot form any OSPF adjacency on that interface
It becomes BDR by default
It is ineligible to become DR or BDR but can still form adjacencies as a DROTHER
It becomes DR whenever it boots first
q: An administrator sets an OSPF interface priority to 0 on a router attached to a broadcast segment that needs a DR and BDR. What is the effect on that router?

explain: No DR/BDR election occurs on point-to-point networks because there are only two routers to synchronize. Equal default priorities do not cause an election failure on broadcast networks either, since router ID breaks the tie.
options: The election failed because both priorities are 1
The DR is hidden and only shown with show ip ospf database
A DR is elected only after the dead timer expires once
Point-to-point networks do not elect a DR or BDR; the two routers form a direct Full adjacency
q: Two routers are linked by a serial point-to-point connection running OSPF. An engineer looks for the DR on this link and finds none. What explains this?

explain: DROTHERs go Full with both the DR and the BDR, so R3-R1 and R3-R2 are Full. R3-R4 stays at Two-Way, and R1-R2 are Full immediately, not only after a failure.
options: R3 with R1
R1 with R2 only if R3 fails
R3 with R4
R3 with R2
q: On a broadcast segment with routers R1 (DR), R2 (BDR), R3 (DROTHER), and R4 (DROTHER), which pairs reach the Full state? (Choose two.)

explain: The FULL/ - display reflects that point-to-point links have no DR role to report, while the adjacency itself is complete. A DROTHER designation would only appear on multi-access networks.
options: The neighbor is a DROTHER
The adjacency is incomplete
The interface is passive
No DR or BDR exists on a point-to-point network type
q: On a point-to-point OSPF link, in the neighbor output the state is shown as FULL/ - with no DR designation. What does the dash indicate?

explain: Router ID selection prefers the highest IP address on a loopback interface over any physical interface address. Physical addresses are used only when no loopback exists.
options: 10.255.255.1, because the highest IP address on a loopback interface is preferred
192.168.1.1, because it was configured first
No router ID is selected until one is configured manually
192.168.1.1, because physical interfaces are preferred
q: A router has a physical interface IP of 192.168.1.1/24, a loopback0 of 10.255.255.1/32, and no manually configured router ID when OSPF starts. Which address becomes the router ID?

explain: With no manual ID and no loopback, the highest IP address on an active physical interface, 192.168.9.1, is selected. The lowest address is never the selection rule.
options: The lowest address, 10.10.10.6, to conserve space
q: A router has no loopback interfaces and no manual router ID. Its active physical interfaces are 172.16.5.2/24, 192.168.9.1/24, and 10.10.10.6/30 at OSPF startup. Which address is chosen as the router ID?

explain: A newly configured router-id does not apply until the OSPF process restarts, via clear ip ospf process or reload. Toggling passive status does not restart the process or change the ID.
options: A second OSPF process must be created with the new ID
The OSPF process must be restarted, for example with clear ip ospf process or a reload
Nothing; the command is rejected if an ID already exists
The interfaces must be changed to passive and back
q: Output excerpt: show ip ospf; Routing Process ospf 1 with ID 10.1.1.1; Supports only single TOS(TOS0) routes. An admin configures router-id 10.9.9.9 under the process to standardize IDs but the output still shows 10.1.1.1. What must happen for the new ID to take effect?

explain: Router IDs must be unique within the routing domain; duplicates cause LSA origination conflicts, warnings, and unstable routing. There is no automatic renumbering to resolve the conflict.
options: The DR election fails but all routes still install correctly
One router automatically increments its ID and continues normally
No effect, because router IDs only need to be unique per link
Adjacency and routing instability, with log warnings about the duplicate ID and LSAs that cannot be distinguished correctly
q: Two routers in the same area are accidentally configured with the same OSPF router ID. What is the most likely observable result?

explain: FULL/DR means the adjacency is fully synchronized and the neighbor fills the DR role, with a live dead timer counting down from hellos. A DROTHER in Two-Way would display 2WAY/DROTHER instead.
options: It is a DROTHER stuck in Two-Way
It is fully adjacent with this router and is the DR for the segment
Its dead timer has expired
It is the BDR for the segment
q: Output excerpt: show ip ospf neighbor; Neighbor ID 10.1.1.2, Pri 1, State FULL/DR, Dead Time 00:00:37, Address 192.168.1.2, Interface GigabitEthernet0/0. What can be concluded about the neighbor at 192.168.1.2?

explain: Broadcast and point-to-point network types default to a 10-second hello and 40-second dead interval. The 30/120 pair is the default for non-broadcast multi-access networks.
options: Hello 5 seconds, dead 20 seconds
Hello 30 seconds, dead 120 seconds
Hello 10 seconds, dead 30 seconds
Hello 10 seconds, dead 40 seconds
q: What are the default OSPF hello and dead intervals on a broadcast Ethernet interface?

explain: Hello and dead intervals are carried in hellos and must match for adjacency; a mismatch prevents neighbor formation entirely. Faster hellos confer no DR advantage.
options: The adjacency does not form because hello and dead timers must match between neighbors
R2 becomes DR automatically because it sends hellos faster
The adjacency forms but updates are sent twice as fast
The adjacency forms in Two-Way and stops there
q: R1 uses a hello interval of 10 seconds on a link while R2 uses 5 seconds on the same link, with all other parameters matching. What is the result?

explain: A neighbor is declared down when the dead interval, 40 seconds by default on broadcast links, expires without a hello. Missing a single hello at 10 seconds does not remove the neighbor.
options: After 40 seconds, the dead interval
After 120 seconds, four hello intervals on NBMA only
After 10 seconds, one hello interval
Immediately when the first hello is missed
q: A working OSPF neighbor stops sending hellos because its interface fails silently. After how long, with default broadcast timers, will the local router declare it down and remove it?

explain: Timer values must agree on both sides; altering one side creates a hello/dead mismatch that blocks adjacency. The command is valid on point-to-point links and is accepted without a reload.
options: The link must be shut and reopened for any timer command to be accepted
Hello-interval can only be changed on broadcast networks
Changing the hello interval changes the derived dead interval expectation, so the two sides disagree on timers and reject each other's hellos
Changing the hello interval also requires changing the router ID
q: An engineer configures ip ospf hello-interval 20 on one side of a point-to-point link but leaves the other side at default. The neighbor never appears. What is the underlying reason?

explain: Passive interfaces send no hellos and form no adjacencies, but their connected network is still advertised by the router's LSA. It controls adjacency formation, not data-plane forwarding or advertisement.
options: It makes the router the DR for that subnet permanently
It suppresses hello packets on that interface so no adjacency forms there, while the connected prefix is still advertised into OSPF
It removes the prefix from the LSDB entirely
It blocks all traffic routed into that subnet
q: An interface is configured as passive under OSPF for subnet 192.168.10.0/24. Users on that subnet still need the prefix reachable from the rest of the OSPF domain. What does the passive setting do?

explain: passive-interface default silences all interfaces, and no passive-interface on the WAN link re-enables hellos only where an adjacency is wanted. Removing network statements would also stop advertising the LAN prefixes, which is not desired.
options: Configure passive-interface default, then no passive-interface on the WAN interface
Set the LAN interface priorities to 0
Remove the network statements for the LAN subnets
Configure passive-interface on the WAN interface only
q: A branch router has four LAN interfaces that should never form OSPF adjacencies and one WAN interface that should. Which configuration approach best achieves this with the least ongoing effort?

explain: Passive suppresses hellos so no adjacency forms, while the prefix is still originated into the LSDB. The interface itself remains up in interface output; passive is an OSPF behavior, not a link state.
options: A passive interface is shown as DOWN in show ip interface brief
A passive interface still sends hello packets but ignores received hellos
A passive interface forms no adjacency on that interface
The connected prefix of a passive interface can still be advertised into OSPF
q: Which two statements about OSPF passive interfaces are true? (Choose two.)

explain: Cost equals reference bandwidth 10^8 bps divided by interface bandwidth, so 100,000,000 / 100,000,000 for Gigabit is 1 and for 100 Mbps FastEthernet it is 10. A cost of 100 would correspond to a 10 Mbps Ethernet link.
q: Using the default reference bandwidth, what is the OSPF cost of a FastEthernet (100 Mbps) interface?

explain: Raising the reference bandwidth makes faster links get lower, distinct costs, but it must be consistent on all routers or path choices become inconsistent. Changing it on one router alone does not fix domain-wide selection.
options: Set every interface cost manually to 1 so all paths are equal
Raise the reference bandwidth consistently on all routers, for example auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
Disable SPF so the first learned path is always kept
Lower the reference bandwidth to 1 Mbps so all links differ
q: With the default reference bandwidth, a 1 Gbps link and a 10 Gbps link both have an OSPF cost of 1, so OSPF treats them as equal. What is the recommended correction?

explain: OSPF sums the outgoing interface costs along each path; 10+10=20 beats 1+50=51, so the two-hop path wins. Hop count is not used by OSPF, so the one-intermediate-hop path does not win on hops.
options: Path B, because its first link has cost 1
Path A, because its cumulative cost of 20 is lower than Path B at 51
Path B, because it has fewer routers to traverse
Both paths equally, because OSPF load-balances all known paths
q: Router R1 can reach a destination via Path A with outgoing interface costs 10 then 10, or via Path B with costs 1 then 50. Which path does OSPF install and why?

explain: The interface output shows cost 10, consistent with the default reference bandwidth divided by 100 Mbps, and the adjacency to the DR is Full. The 40-second value is the dead interval derived from timers, not the cost.
options: The interface cost is 40
The interface cost is 10 and the neighbor adjacency to the DR is Full
The reference bandwidth has been raised to 10 Gbps
The interface is the DR
q: Output excerpt: show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/1; Internet Address 192.168.2.1/24, Area 0; Process ID 1, Router ID 10.0.0.1; Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 10; Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State BDR; Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5; Neighbor Count is 2, Adjacent neighbor count is 2; Adjacent with neighbor 10.0.0.2 (Designated Router). What is correct about this interface?

explain: Cost is reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, and raising the reference bandwidth differentiates gigabit-and-faster links. Cost is based on bandwidth, not latency or load, and it should be changed consistently.
options: The reference bandwidth can safely be set differently on each router in an area
OSPF cost is based primarily on measured round-trip latency
OSPF cost is calculated as reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth
Increasing the reference bandwidth allows links faster than 100 Mbps to receive distinct costs
q: Which two statements about OSPF cost and reference bandwidth are true? (Choose two.)

explain: Every OSPF router originates its own Type 1 router LSA describing its links, and it floods only within its area. Type 1 LSAs are not originated by the DR alone; the DR originates the Type 2 for the transit network.
options: Only ASBRs, describing external routes
Only ABRs, summarizing other areas
Only the DR, describing the entire broadcast network
Every router in the area, describing its own connected links and neighbors
q: At CCNA depth, who originates a Type 1 router LSA in OSPF and what is its flooding scope?

explain: The DR originates the Type 2 network LSA for a transit broadcast network, listing the attached routers. DROTHERs do not originate Type 2 LSAs for the segment.
options: The DR, describing the multi-access network and its attached routers
The BDR, as a backup copy of the DR data
The ABR, summarizing the network to the backbone
Any DROTHER that boots first
q: On a broadcast segment, which router originates the Type 2 network LSA and what does it represent?

explain: Type 3 summary LSAs are originated by ABRs to advertise prefixes from one area into another. They are not external routes; external prefixes use Type 5 LSAs originated by ASBRs.
options: An ABR, for prefixes from one area advertised into another area
An ASBR, for external prefixes redistributed into OSPF
The DR, for routers on a broadcast segment
Every router, for its own directly connected links
q: A prefix learned from Area 1 appears in Area 0 routers as an inter-area route. Which LSA type carried it into Area 0 and who originated it?

explain: Within a single area all routers run SPF on an identical LSDB for that area, which is why their intra-area view is consistent. Routers in different areas do not share identical LSDBs.
options: They elect a single DR for the whole area
They have identical routing tables in all cases
They have an identical LSDB for that area
They share the same router ID format only
q: Two routers are in the same single OSPF area and have completed adjacency formation with all neighbors. What must be true about their link-state databases for that area?

explain: A single area keeps design simple for small networks, while multiarea reduces LSDB and SPF load per area as the network grows. Multiarea does not remove the need for a DR on broadcast segments or make all adjacencies point-to-point.
options: Single-area OSPF is simple and appropriate for small networks
Single-area OSPF requires every router to be an ABR
Multiarea OSPF can reduce LSDB size and SPF workload within each area in a large network
Multiarea OSPF eliminates the need for a DR on broadcast networks
q: Which two statements correctly contrast single-area and multiarea OSPF? (Choose two.)

explain: In multiarea OSPF all non-backbone areas must attach to Area 0, directly or via a virtual link, so summaries flow through the backbone. Placing the new area as a standalone backbone would partition the domain.
options: Attach it to any existing area, because OSPF floods summaries area to area freely
Make it Area 0 as well and merge the two backbones later
Connect it to Area 0, the backbone, directly or through a virtual link
Leave it unconnected until it contains at least two ABRs
q: A design grows from single-area OSPF to multiarea. A new Area 10 is added for a remote site. How must Area 10 connect for inter-area routing to work in the standard design?

explain: A wildcard of 0.0.0.0 requires an exact address match, so only the interface with 10.0.0.1 is enabled for area 0. A wildcard of 0.0.0.255 would have matched a whole /24 range instead.
options: All interfaces in 10.0.0.0/24
Only the interface whose address is exactly 10.0.0.1
All interfaces in 10.0.0.0/8
No interfaces, because the wildcard is invalid
q: A router is configured with network 10.0.0.1 0.0.0.0 area 0 under OSPF. The router has interfaces addressed 10.0.0.1/24, 10.0.0.2/24, and 10.0.1.1/24. Which interfaces are enabled for OSPF area 0 by this statement?

explain: Wildcard 0.0.0.255 ignores the last octet, so any 192.168.1.x interface address matches and is placed in area 0. It does not match 192.168.2.x because the third octet must still equal 1.
options: All 192.168.x.x interfaces
q: A router has interfaces 192.168.1.1/24, 192.168.1.2/24 on a second interface, and 192.168.2.1/24. It is configured with network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0. Which interfaces run OSPF in area 0?

explain: Network statements enable OSPF only on interfaces whose addresses match; an unmatched address means the interface sends no hellos, which show ip ospf interface confirms. The link being up rules out a physical cause.
options: The router ID is not on a loopback
The DR on the segment has failed
The network statement wildcard does not match the interface address, so OSPF is not enabled on that interface
The interface priority is too low
q: An OSPF interface is up/up with a correct IP address, area and timers match the neighbor, yet show ip ospf interface does not list the interface at all and no neighbor forms. What is the most likely configuration cause?

explain: Wildcard mask is the inverse of the subnet mask: 255.255.255.240 inverts to 0.0.0.15, matching exactly 16 addresses. Using the subnet mask itself as the wildcard would match a far larger, wrong range.
q: An engineer needs a network statement to match interfaces in subnet 172.16.8.16/28, whose subnet mask is 255.255.255.240. What wildcard mask should be used?

explain: 2WAY/DROTHER is the expected steady state between two DROTHERs on a broadcast network, not a failure. Full is only required toward the DR and BDR.
options: The routers are stuck in Exchange
This is the normal state between two DROTHER routers on a broadcast network
The neighbor is down and the dead timer will remove it
This neighbor is the DR but has not finished loading
q: Output excerpt: show ip ospf neighbor; Neighbor ID 10.1.1.3, Pri 1, State 2WAY/DROTHER, Dead Time 00:00:32, Address 192.168.1.3, Interface GigabitEthernet0/0. The local router is also a DROTHER on this segment. How should this output be interpreted?

explain: The output shows the interface itself is DR, there is no BDR yet on the segment, and its cost is 1, consistent with a gigabit link at default reference bandwidth. BDR status would be shown as State BDR, not DR.
options: State DR, Cost: 1
State BDR, Cost: 10
State POINT-TO-POINT, Cost: 10
State DROTHER, Cost: 1
q: Output excerpt: show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0; Internet Address 192.168.1.1/24, Area 0; Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1; State DR, Priority 1; Designated Router (ID) 10.0.0.1, Interface address 192.168.1.1; Backup Designated Router (ID) 0.0.0.0; Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40. What does this output show about the local router on this segment?

explain: O marks intra-area OSPF routes and O IA marks inter-area routes learned via Type 3 summaries from an ABR. E2 would denote an external Type 5 route, not an inter-area one.
options: O denotes a directly connected route learned by OSPF
O denotes an OSPF external route and O IA an internal static route
O denotes a static route and O IA a default route
O denotes an intra-area OSPF route and O IA denotes an inter-area OSPF route
q: Output excerpt: show ip route ospf; O 10.2.2.0/24 [110/20] via 192.168.1.2, 00:12:03, GigabitEthernet0/0; O IA 10.5.5.0/24 [110/30] via 192.168.1.2, 00:12:03, GigabitEthernet0/0. What distinguishes the second route from the first?

explain: Routers must be in the same area on a common link to become neighbors; an area mismatch blocks adjacency before any LSA exchange. Different process IDs, by contrast, are locally significant and do not block adjacency.
options: Different OSPF process IDs
One router having an extra passive LAN interface
Different router ID formats, one from a loopback and one manual
Mismatched area IDs on the connecting interfaces
q: Two routers are cabled together, their interfaces are in the same subnet with matching timers and MTU, but no neighbor ever appears. On inspection, one interface is assigned to area 0 and the other to area 5. What prevents adjacency?

explain: On broadcast networks neighbors must agree on the subnet mask in hellos; a /24 versus /25 mismatch causes hellos to be rejected and no adjacency forms. A passive interface would still list in protocol output, which is not described here.
options: Mismatched router IDs in the same octet
Mismatched subnet masks in the hello packets on a broadcast network
Mismatched process IDs
Mismatched OSPF priorities
q: On a broadcast link, R1 has address 192.168.1.1/24 and R2 has 192.168.1.2/25, with matching timers, area, and MTU. Hellos are sent by both but no adjacency forms. What is the most likely cause?

explain: When authentication is configured, mismatched types or keys cause hello authentication failures and neighbors never form. The debug message type points directly to authentication rather than timer values, which are not mentioned as mismatched.
options: The routers are in different areas
The DR election is incomplete
The reference bandwidth differs
An OSPF authentication mismatch, such as different keys or authentication types
q: After enabling OSPF authentication on one router of a working pair but not correctly on the other, the adjacency drops and debug output reports authentication failures on received hellos. What must be corrected?

explain: Interface-level ip ospf process-id area enables OSPF on that interface directly, without needing a matching network statement for it. The network statement is not converted automatically; the interface command is the configuration present on the interface.
options: OSPF is enabled on that interface in area 0 by the interface command itself
The command only works on loopback interfaces
The command puts the interface in passive mode
The interface will not run OSPF because a network statement is mandatory
q: Instead of a network statement, an interface is configured with ip ospf 1 area 0. What is the result for that interface?

explain: show ip protocols reveals the networks and areas being routed for, the router ID, and passive interfaces in one view. Neighbor state detail belongs to show ip ospf neighbor, not this command.
options: The cost of every OSPF path in the routing table
The routing protocol in use, its networks and areas, the router ID, and which interfaces are passive
The DR and BDR for every segment and each neighbor state
The full LSDB contents for area 0
q: Output excerpt: show ip protocols; Routing Protocol is ospf 1; Outgoing update filter list for all interfaces is not set; Router ID 10.0.0.1; Number of areas in this router is 1; Routing for Networks: 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0; Passive Interface(s): GigabitEthernet0/2. Which verification need does this command best satisfy?

explain: In HSRP the active router forwards for the virtual IP/MAC while the standby monitors and is ready to take over if hellos stop. No forwarding for the virtual address is done by the standby while the active is healthy.
options: The active router forwards traffic sent to the virtual IP and MAC, while the standby waits to take over if the active fails
The active router only sends hellos and never forwards
The standby router forwards half the traffic for the virtual IP
Both routers forward using the virtual MAC simultaneously
q: Two routers run HSRP for a LAN subnet with a virtual IP used as the hosts' default gateway. What are the roles of the active and standby routers while both are healthy?

explain: HSRP version 1 uses 0000.0c07.acXX where XX is the group in hex; group 10 decimal is 0x0A, giving 0000.0c07.ac0a. The 0000.0c9f.f prefix belongs to version 2.
q: A LAN uses HSRP version 1, group 10. Which virtual MAC address will hosts learn for the virtual gateway?

explain: HSRPv2 virtual MACs use 0000.0c9f.fXXX with the group encoded in the last three hex digits, so group 1 is 0000.0c9f.f001. The 0000.0c07.ac prefix is version 1 and 0000.5e00.01 is VRRP.
q: A gateway group is migrated to HSRP version 2, group 1. Which virtual MAC address should now be expected for the group?

explain: HSRPv2 expands groups to 0-4095 and uses multicast 224.0.0.102, while v1 uses 224.0.0.2 and groups 0-255. The virtual MAC formats also differ, so v1 and v2 in the same group do not interoperate.
options: HSRP version 2 uses multicast address 224.0.0.102 for hellos
HSRP version 1 and version 2 use the same virtual MAC format and interoperate in a group
HSRP version 1 supports group numbers 0 through 4095
HSRP version 2 supports group numbers 0 through 4095
q: Which two statements about HSRP versions are true? (Choose two.)

explain: HSRP preempt is disabled by default, so a returning higher-priority router stays standby until preempt is configured or the active fails. Priority alone does not force an immediate takeover.
options: It remains standby unless preempt is configured on it
It forces a new election in which the lower-priority router wins
It takes over immediately because it has higher priority
It shuts down the virtual IP until manually cleared
q: An HSRP active router with priority 100 fails and its standby with priority 90 takes over. The original router returns with priority 100 but its interface has no preempt configured. What happens?

explain: The output shows only one Active and R2 as Standby, so R1 is forwarding for the virtual IP. There is no indication of tracking or authentication failure in this brief output.
options: R1 is the active router and R2 is standby for group 1
Group 1 has failed because two routers are listed
The virtual IP is owned by whichever host sends ARP first
R2 is active because it is listed first in the output
q: Output excerpt: show standby brief; P indicates configured to preempt; Interface Grp Pri P State Active Standby Virtual IP; Gi0/0 1 110 P Active local 192.168.1.3 192.168.1.254, shown on router R1 whose address is 192.168.1.2. What does this output establish?

explain: The default HSRP priority is 100, and when priorities tie the router with the higher interface IP address becomes active. The lower IP address does not win the tie.
options: 50, and the lowest IP address wins ties
90, and the router that boots last wins ties
110, and the lowest router ID wins ties
100, and the highest interface IP address wins ties
q: Two HSRP routers have no priority configured. What is their default priority, and how is the active router decided between them?

explain: VRRP uses virtual MAC 0000.5e00.01XX with the VRID in the last byte, so group 10 is 0000.5e00.010a. The 0000.0c07.ac prefix is HSRP version 1, not VRRP.
options: 0100.5e00.010a as a locally administered real MAC
q: A subnet uses VRRP group (VRID) 10 for gateway redundancy. Which virtual MAC address will the master advertise for the virtual IP?

explain: VRRP enables preemption by default, so a returning higher-priority master candidate reclaims the master role after its startup delay. This contrasts with HSRP, where preempt must be explicitly configured.
options: It forms a second master and both forward permanently
It stays backup until an administrator manually forces mastership
It becomes master again because VRRP preemption is enabled by default
It can never become master again once it has failed
q: A VRRP master with priority 120 fails and the backup takes over. The original router recovers with its priority of 120 while the current master has priority 100, and no preempt settings have been changed from defaults. What happens in VRRP?

explain: In VRRP only the master responds to ARP for and forwards traffic to the virtual IP; backups listen for advertisements and take over if they stop. Backups do not forward for the virtual IP while a master is healthy.
options: All backups forward traffic equally with the master
The backup with the lowest IP forwards while the master only advertises
Mastership rotates to a different router every advertisement interval
Only the master forwards for the virtual IP, while backups monitor its advertisements
q: In a VRRP group with one master and two backups, all healthy, how is forwarding for the virtual IP handled?

explain: The AVG assigns virtual MACs and answers ARP, while AVFs forward traffic for an assigned virtual MAC, and one router can hold both roles. GLBP does not use a single active forwarder for all traffic as HSRP does.
options: GLBP elects a DR that builds an LSDB for the group
The AVG forwards all traffic and AVFs only send hellos
Every GLBP router is a standby that never forwards
One router is elected AVG to assign virtual MACs and answer ARP, while routers acting as AVFs forward traffic for their assigned virtual MACs
q: A LAN is configured with GLBP instead of HSRP to use both uplinks. What are the roles of the AVG and the AVFs?

explain: GLBP supports round-robin, weighted, and host-dependent distribution of clients across AVFs. It does not send all traffic through one forwarder; that single-forwarder behavior describes HSRP.
options: Weighted, where AVFs receive a share of hosts proportional to their configured weighting
Round-robin, where successive hosts are assigned virtual MACs of different AVFs in turn
Single-forwarder, where all hosts always receive the same virtual MAC
Per-packet spraying of one host's packets across all AVFs for a single flow
q: Which two load-balancing methods are valid GLBP forwarding methods? (Choose two.)

explain: GLBP deliberately gives different hosts different gateway virtual MACs so multiple AVFs forward simultaneously, unlike HSRP where only the active forwards for the group. Hosts still use the same virtual IP as their gateway.
options: Normal only if the hosts are in different VLANs
A fault; GLBP must return the same virtual MAC to every host
Normal GLBP behavior; different hosts can receive different AVF virtual MACs for the same virtual IP so multiple routers forward at once
A sign the AVG has failed and an AVF is rogue
q: With GLBP running, two hosts in the same VLAN ARP for their default gateway virtual IP and receive different virtual MAC addresses in the replies. Both can reach remote networks. How should this be interpreted?

explain: HSRP routers must agree on group number and version to operate as one group; a version mismatch splits them into separate groups that each claim active. A priority difference alone is expected and does not cause dual-active by itself.
options: Their hello timers differ by a small amount but are within tolerance
One router runs HSRP version 1 and the other version 2 for the same group, so they do not recognize each other as group members
One router has a loopback interface configured
Their priorities differ, which always produces two actives
q: Two routers should form one HSRP group for a VLAN, but both claim the Active state and hosts see flapping gateway MAC responses. Priorities are 110 and 100 as designed. What configuration mismatch most likely explains the dual-active state?

explain: Tracking decrements the HSRP priority by 20 when the WAN link fails, dropping R1 to 90, below the standby's 100, and preempt on the standby lets it take over. Without the decrement, R1 would keep the higher configured priority despite losing upstream connectivity.
options: Priority 110, because tracking never changes the effective priority
Priority 90, allowing the standby at priority 100 with preempt to become active
Priority 100, exactly tying the standby so the higher IP wins
Priority 0, because a tracked failure disables HSRP entirely
q: An HSRP active router has priority 110 and tracks its WAN interface with a decrement of 20. The standby has priority 100 and preempt enabled. The WAN interface fails. What is the active router's effective priority and the expected outcome?

explain: IPv6 statics use ipv6 route followed by the destination prefix and the global unicast next hop. The IPv4 ip route command and an IPv4 next hop cannot install an IPv6 route.
q: An administrator must add an IPv6 static route to prefix 2001:db8:2::/64 via global next hop 2001:db8:1::2. Which command is correct?

explain: Link-local addresses exist on every link, so the router must be told which exit interface to use with a link-local next hop. A global next hop does not need this because it is uniquely routable.
options: The exit interface must also be specified because a link-local address is only meaningful on a specific link
The next hop must be rewritten as a global address by NAT66
Link-local next hops are prohibited in static routes
The route must also specify a metric of 0
q: A static IPv6 route is configured as ipv6 route 2001:db8:3::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0 fe80::1. Why is the exit interface included along with next hop fe80::1?

explain: The higher AD of 10 makes the second static a floating backup that only installs when the primary route with AD 1 disappears. Without the AD value both statics would install at AD 1 and load-balance instead.
options: It converts the primary route into a floating route as well
It replaces the primary route immediately because it was configured last
It stays out of the routing table while the AD 1 route is present and installs only if that primary route is lost
It is permanently rejected as a duplicate prefix
q: A router has ipv6 route 2001:db8:4::/64 2001:db8:1::2 and an engineer adds ipv6 route 2001:db8:4::/64 2001:db8:9::2 10. What is the purpose and behavior of the second route?

explain: A fully specified static names both the exit interface and the next hop, removing any ambiguity about where to forward. Specifying only a link-local next hop without the interface leaves the link ambiguous.
options: It names both the exit interface and the next-hop address
It names only a link-local next hop
It names two different destination prefixes
It includes both an AD and a permanent keyword in all cases
q: Which configuration describes a fully specified IPv6 static route?

explain: The S code denotes a static route and the entry shows the global next hop and exit interface it resolves through. A C code would denote a directly connected prefix, not the static entry described.
options: It is a route learned from NDP neighbor discovery
It is a connected route learned from an interface address
It is a static route to 2001:db8:5::/64 via 2001:db8:1::2 out GigabitEthernet0/0
It is the local host route for the interface itself
q: Output excerpt: show ipv6 route; S 2001:DB8:5::/64 [1/0]; via 2001:DB8:1::2, GigabitEthernet0/0; C 2001:DB8:1::/64 [0/0]; via GigabitEthernet0/0, directly connected. What does the first entry represent?

explain: The interface is up/up with both a global and a link-local address, so it can forward IPv6 and be used by statics. An interface showing only a link-local address would lack the global prefix assignment seen here.
options: The interface is administratively down
The interface has no link-local address
The interface is up, has global address 2001:db8:1::1/64 and link-local fe80::1, and can route IPv6
