explain: A VPN creates a private, protected tunnel over a public network so sensitive data can travel confidentially. It does not physically replace the internet or remove authentication; users and gateways must still authenticate.
options: It replaces the public internet with a physically private line
It removes the need for any authentication of remote users
It guarantees the internet path will never be congested
It creates a private, encrypted connection over a public network
q: A business must send sensitive data between locations but can only use the public internet for transport. Leaders ask what fundamental problem a VPN solves in this situation. Which answer is correct?

explain: ESP provides encryption for confidentiality and IKE negotiates the security associations IPsec uses. AH provides no encryption, and GRE alone provides encapsulation without encryption, so those two statements are false.
options: AH provides confidentiality through encryption of the payload
IKE negotiates security associations for IPsec
GRE alone provides strong encryption for tunneled data
ESP can provide confidentiality through encryption
q: Which two statements about VPNs and IPsec are correct at a CCNA level? (Choose two.)

explain: A stateful firewall tracks connection state and permits return traffic belonging to established sessions. A stateless filter judges each packet in isolation, so it cannot recognize return traffic as part of an inside-initiated connection.
options: An IDS that only logs suspicious traffic
A host-based antivirus function
Stateful inspection that tracks connection state
Stateless packet filtering with no connection tracking
q: A small office firewall inspects traffic and allows return traffic for connections initiated from inside, while blocking unsolicited inbound connections. Which firewall behavior is described?

explain: A next-generation firewall adds application awareness, deep inspection, and threat intelligence beyond basic stateful filtering. A passive IDS only detects and alerts, and does not enforce firewall policy in the traffic path.
options: A passive IDS sensor
A syslog server
A stateless packet filter
A next-generation firewall
q: A vendor describes a security appliance that combines traditional firewall functions with application awareness, deep inspection, and integrated threat intelligence. Which category best fits this description?

explain: An IDS monitors copied traffic out of band and alerts, but cannot block traffic because it is not in the forwarding path. An IPS sits inline specifically so it can drop malicious traffic, which this placement cannot do.
options: An NGFW in routed mode
An IPS in inline mode
A stateful firewall at the perimeter
An IDS in passive monitoring mode
q: A sensor is placed on a SPAN port so it can analyze a copy of network traffic and generate alerts, but it cannot block malicious packets itself. Which system is deployed?

explain: An IPS sits inline and can block malicious traffic in real time. An IDS on a SPAN port sees only a copy and can alert but cannot prevent the original packet from reaching the server.
options: An IDS on a SPAN port
An IPS placed inline
A syslog collector in the data center
A network time server with logging enabled
q: An organization requires a security device positioned inline in the traffic flow so malicious traffic can be dropped before it reaches a server, not merely logged after the fact. Which system meets this requirement?

explain: An IDS passively monitors copied traffic and alerts, while an IPS is inline and can block traffic. An IDS on a SPAN port cannot drop original packets, and an IPS that never affects flow would defeat its prevention purpose.
options: An IPS is placed inline so it can drop malicious traffic
An IPS must always be passive so it never affects traffic flow
An IDS can monitor a copy of traffic via a SPAN port without being in the forwarding path
An IDS placed on a SPAN port can drop packets before they reach a host
q: A designer must place detection and prevention controls correctly in a new network. Which two placements are correct? (Choose two.)

explain: Defense in depth layers independent controls so the failure of one does not expose the asset completely. Duplicating one firewall is redundancy, not layered diversity, and no single control makes training, patching, or policies unnecessary.
options: Layered security removes the need for any security policies
A single firewall, if stateful, makes user training and patching unnecessary
Layered controls ensure that if one control fails or is bypassed, other controls still protect assets
Defense in depth means buying two identical firewalls from the same vendor
q: During a design review, an architect argues for defense in depth rather than relying on a single perimeter firewall to stop every attack. Which reasoning best supports that position?

explain: A security program includes people and governance elements such as awareness training and documented, communicated policies. A single AAA server or VPN tunnel is a technical control, not the program itself.
options: A single TACACS+ server configured for device login
One IPsec tunnel configured between two gateways
Documented security policies that staff are made aware of
Ongoing user awareness training for all staff
q: Which two elements belong to a complete organizational security program rather than to a single technical control? (Choose two.)

explain: MFA defeats a sprayed correct password, and blocking common passwords removes the small set spraying depends on. Unlimited attempts help the attacker, and shared passwords widen the impact of a single guess.
options: Blocking commonly used passwords in the password policy
Enforcing MFA for remote access accounts
Allowing each account unlimited failed login attempts
Using one shared password for all service accounts
q: Which two practices most directly reduce the success of password spraying against internet-facing services? (Choose two.)

explain: Numbers 100-199 (and 2000-2699) are extended ACLs, which can match protocol and ports. Standard ACLs use 1-99 and 1300-1999 and cannot match a TCP port at all.
options: An extended numbered ACL, because 110 is in the 100-199 extended range
A standard numbered ACL, because 110 is in the 1-99 standard range expanded by 10
A standard numbered ACL, because only the source is checked before the port
A named standard ACL, because a host keyword is used
q: A junior engineer configures 'access-list 110 permit tcp any host 10.2.2.10 eq 443' on a router and asks what kind of ACL she has just created. Which answer is correct?

explain: ACL 45 falls in the 1-99 standard range, so it can match source address only. Port or destination matching requires an extended ACL (100-199 or 2000-2699), not a name change.
options: ACL 45 is reserved for VTY lines, so interface filtering options are hidden
ACL 45 is a standard ACL, and standard ACLs match only the source IP address
ACL 45 is an extended ACL, and extended ACLs match ports only with the range keyword
ACL 45 must be converted to a named ACL before any entry can be saved
q: A technician writes ACL 45 to block traffic from 192.168.5.0/24 and then tries to add an entry matching destination port 25, but the router will not accept port matching in that ACL. Why?

explain: Standard ACLs match source only, so placing one near the source would block Sales from all destinations. Placing it close to the destination limits the collateral damage; extended ACLs are the ones placed close to the source.
options: As close to the destination server as possible, so it blocks only traffic headed to that destination area
As close to the source Sales subnet as possible, on the branch router LAN interface
Only on the VTY lines of the HQ router, because the traffic is management traffic
On every WAN interface in the path, so the first router drops the traffic earliest
q: A branch design must stop one server, and only that server, from being reached by the Sales subnet, while Sales still reaches every other server at HQ. A standard ACL is chosen so only the source can be judged. Where should that standard ACL be placed?

explain: Extended ACLs can identify the exact traffic, so they are placed close to the source to drop unwanted packets early. Placing a standard ACL near the source would be risky, but an extended ACL can surgically deny only Telnet.
options: Only as an outbound ACL on every core interface at HQ
Close to the source contractor subnet, before the traffic crosses the WAN
Close to the destination servers, inbound on the server-farm interface
On the VTY lines of the contractor router, because Telnet is a VTY protocol
q: An extended ACL will deny Telnet from a contractor subnet to all internal hosts while permitting the contractor's other traffic. To save WAN bandwidth and stop the traffic early, where should the ACL be applied?

explain: Standard ACLs match source address only and use 1-99 plus the expanded 1300-1999 range. Port matching belongs to extended ACLs, and standard ACLs are normally applied with ip access-group, though they can also be used on VTY lines.
options: It can match TCP and UDP destination port numbers
Numbered standard ACLs use the ranges 1-99 and 1300-1999
It must always be applied with the access-class command
It matches packets based on source IP address only
q: Which two statements correctly describe a standard IPv4 ACL? (Choose two.)

explain: A /24 has a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0, so the wildcard is its inverse, 0.0.0.255, meaning the last octet can vary. Using 255.255.255.0 as the wildcard would instead ignore the first 24 bits and require the last octet to be 0.
q: A network administrator must write an extended ACL entry that permits traffic from the entire 172.20.8.0/24 subnet. Which wildcard mask completes the entry 'permit ip 172.20.8.0 ___ any'?

explain: The host keyword means a wildcard of 0.0.0.0, so every bit must match and only 10.10.10.9 is permitted as the source. A 0.0.0.255 wildcard would permit the whole /24, and the third option puts the server in the destination field instead.
options: permit ip any host 10.10.10.9
permit ip host 10.10.10.9 any
q: An ACL entry must permit exactly one server, 10.10.10.9, and no other host. Which entry does that?

explain: Wildcard 1 bits are ignored and 0 bits must match, so 255.255.255.0 ignores the first 24 bits and requires the last octet to equal 0. The intended /24 match needed wildcard 0.0.0.255.
options: Only the single host 10.20.30.0
Any source address whose last octet is 0, regardless of the first three octets
No sources at all, because IOS rejects a wildcard that starts with 255
Only sources in 10.20.30.0/24
q: By mistake, an engineer enters 'permit ip 10.20.30.0 255.255.255.0 any' using the subnet mask in place of the wildcard mask. Which sources will this entry actually match?

explain: ACLs are processed top-down and the first match wins, so the Telnet packet hits the line 10 deny and never reaches line 20. Line 20 would permit other traffic, but it is not consulted after a match.
options: It is denied by the implicit deny, because no permit line matches it
It is denied, because line 10 matches first and processing stops
It is permitted, because line 20 permits all IP traffic
It is permitted, because the deny applies only to UDP port 23
q: Exhibit: Line 10: deny tcp host 10.1.1.5 any eq 23; Line 20: permit ip any any. The ACL is applied inbound on the LAN interface. A packet arrives from 10.1.1.5 to 10.9.9.20 using TCP destination port 23. What happens to it?

explain: Line 10 matches only TCP port 23 from that host, so a port 80 packet falls through to line 20, which permits any IP traffic. The deny is narrower than it first looks because of the eq 23 condition.
options: It is denied, because line 10 denies all traffic from 10.1.1.5
It is permitted, because line 10 does not match port 80 and line 20 permits all IP traffic
It is denied by the implicit deny, because HTTP was not named in line 10
It is permitted only if the packet also carries the established keyword flag
q: Exhibit: Line 10: deny tcp host 10.1.1.5 any eq 23; Line 20: permit ip any any. The ACL is applied inbound on the LAN interface. A packet arrives from 10.1.1.5 to 10.9.9.20 using TCP destination port 80. What happens to it?

explain: Every ACL ends with an invisible implicit deny any, so unmatched packets are dropped even though no deny was configured. The tempting permit-by-default idea is wrong; only matched permits pass.
options: It is permitted, because an ACL with no explicit deny defaults to permit all
It is routed normally, because unapplied entries are ignored at the end of the list
It is denied by the implicit deny any at the end of every ACL
It is permitted after being logged, because the router assumes it is return traffic
q: An ACL contains a single entry permitting traffic from the management subnet, and no deny entry was ever typed. A packet arrives from a different subnet that matches no entry. What is its fate, and why?

explain: Only ports 80 and 25 are permitted, so the port 443 packet matches no line and falls to the implicit deny. Lines 10 and 20 are permits for their own ports only; they do not deny or permit anything else.
options: The connection is permitted, because HTTPS is matched by the port 25 mail entry
The connection is denied by line 10, which acts as an explicit deny for other ports
The connection is permitted, because line 10 permits all web traffic including HTTPS
The connection is denied by the implicit deny, because neither line matches port 443
q: Exhibit: Line 10: permit tcp 10.4.0.0 0.0.255.255 any eq 80; Line 20: permit tcp 10.4.0.0 0.0.255.255 any eq 25. The ACL is applied inbound toward the internet edge. A user at 10.4.2.7 opens an HTTPS connection to a web server on TCP port 443. What happens?

explain: In ACL subconfiguration mode you can add an entry with any unused sequence number, such as 15, to place it between 10 and 20. Rebuilding the whole ACL works but is unnecessary and risks an open window while no ACL exists.
options: Add the entry at the global prompt with sequence number 5 so it is inserted at the top automatically by IOS sorting
Use the global command 'no access-list' and then retype the entire ACL including the new line
Renumber line 20 to line 15 with the edit command, then append the new entry at the end
Enter ACL configuration mode with 'ip access-list extended <name>' and type the new entry beginning with a sequence number such as 15
q: A named extended ACL has lines 10 and 20, and an administrator must insert a new deny between them without deleting and rebuilding the whole list. What is the correct method?

explain: Inside ACL configuration mode, 'no' followed by a sequence number deletes only that entry. The global 'no access-list' form removes the entire ACL, which is more than the task allows.
options: In ACL configuration mode, enter 'no 20' to delete just the entry with sequence number 20
Enter 'clear access-list counters' so line 20 is flushed from the running configuration
On the interface, enter 'no ip access-group' so line 20 stops being processed
At the global prompt, enter 'no access-list <name>' and re-add lines 10 and 30
q: An engineer must remove only line 20 from a named ACL while leaving lines 10 and 30 active. Which approach does that?

explain: Named ACLs are created with 'ip access-list extended <name>' (or standard), which also drops you into the mode where sequence-number editing works. The numbered 'access-list' command cannot take a name, and a standard named ACL still cannot match ports.
options: access-class BLOCK-GUEST extended in line vty 0 4
access-list BLOCK-GUEST extended permit ip any any
ip access-list standard BLOCK-GUEST, then add port matching inside it
ip access-list extended BLOCK-GUEST
q: A security policy calls for a named extended ACL called BLOCK-GUEST that will be maintained over time with per-line edits and remarks. Which command creates it correctly?

explain: The global command 'ip access-list resequence <name> <starting> <increment>' renumbers the entries, here to 10, 20, 30, 40. It changes only numbering, not the order or content of the entries.
options: ip access-list resequence <name> 5 5, entered in ACL configuration mode
access-list <name> renumber 10 10, entered at the global prompt
resequence access-list <name> 10 10, entered on each interface using it
ip access-list resequence <name> 10 10, entered at the global configuration prompt
q: After months of edits, a named ACL has sequence numbers 10, 13, 17, and 42, making future inserts awkward. Which command renumbers it starting at 10 in steps of 10?

explain: Interface filtering uses 'ip access-group <acl> in|out' under the interface itself. Access-class is for VTY lines, and the access-group command does not exist at the global prompt.
options: In line configuration mode: 'ip access-group 101 in' under line vty 0 4
In global configuration mode: 'ip access-group 101 in'
In interface configuration mode for Gi0/0: 'ip access-group 101 in'
In interface configuration mode for Gi0/0: 'access-class 101 in'
q: ACL 101 is built to filter traffic entering a router from the LAN on GigabitEthernet0/0. Which configuration actually activates it for that direction?

explain: VTY access is controlled with 'access-class <acl> in' in line configuration mode, which checks the source of sessions to the router itself. Ip access-group belongs on interfaces and filters through-traffic, not sessions terminating on the box.
options: Under line vty 0 4: 'access-class 12 in'
In global mode: 'access-class 12 out' so outbound replies are filtered instead
Under line vty 0 4: 'ip access-group 12 in'
Under Gi0/0: 'ip access-group 12 in', because all management traffic enters that interface
q: Only hosts in 10.99.0.0/24 may open SSH or Telnet sessions to a router itself; standard ACL 12 already permits that subnet. Which configuration enforces this on the management lines?

explain: An ACL only inspects traffic crossing the interface and direction it is applied to; this packet never exits Gi0/0, so the ACL never evaluates it. The lines themselves are fine, which is why the tempting line-tracing answers fail: the placement and direction are the defect.
options: The packet is denied by line 10, because ACLs check traffic in both directions once applied to any interface
The packet is denied by the implicit deny after line 20 fails to match it
The packet is not checked by this ACL at all, because it enters Gi0/0 inbound and leaves Gi0/1, never exiting Gi0/0
The packet is permitted by line 20 after line 10 is skipped for being outbound-only
q: Exhibit: Line 10: deny tcp any host 203.0.113.50 eq 80; Line 20: permit ip any any. The ACL is applied outbound on Gi0/0, the LAN-facing interface, while the web server 203.0.113.50 is reached out Gi0/1. A LAN user sends a packet to 203.0.113.50 on TCP port 80. What happens?

explain: Evaluation is strictly top-down with first match wins, so the specific host permit on line 10 fires before the subnet deny is ever reached. ACLs do not reorder by specificity the way some administrators expect.
options: It is denied by the implicit deny, because lines 10 and 20 cancel each other out
It is permitted, because line 10 matches the specific host first, before the subnet deny on line 20
It is permitted by line 30, because the router evaluates permits before denies
It is denied, because the subnet deny on line 20 is broader and broader rules override specific ones
q: Exhibit: Line 10: permit tcp host 192.168.1.10 host 10.5.5.5 eq 443; Line 20: deny tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.5.5.5 eq 443; Line 30: permit ip any any. The ACL is applied inbound on the user LAN. A packet from 192.168.1.10 to 10.5.5.5 on TCP port 443 arrives. What happens?

explain: DHCP is UDP (client port 68, server port 67), and the ACL permits only TCP 80 and 443, so Discover packets fall to the implicit deny. Fixing it requires an explicit UDP permit for DHCP, not moving the same ACL to the outbound direction.
options: DHCP uses TCP ports 67 and 68, so line 10 should have matched it but the server is down
The implicit deny does not apply to broadcast traffic, so the cause must be a cabling fault
DHCP Discover traffic is UDP from port 68 to port 67, matches neither TCP permit, and is dropped by the implicit deny
DHCP leases fail because the ACL must be applied outbound on the VLAN interface instead of inbound
q: Exhibit: Line 10: permit tcp any any eq 80; Line 20: permit tcp any any eq 443. The ACL is applied inbound on the user VLAN interface, and nothing else filters this traffic. PCs on that VLAN suddenly cannot obtain DHCP leases, although web browsing worked before the ACL for users who already have addresses. Why did DHCP break?

explain: IOS ACLs are not stateful for UDP, and both permit lines match TCP only, so the UDP DNS reply hits the implicit deny. A permit for UDP source port 53 return traffic (or DNS inspection elsewhere) is needed; assuming return traffic is automatic is the classic mistake.
options: It is permitted, because return traffic for an outbound request is always allowed by IOS ACLs
It is permitted by line 10, because DNS uses port 80 for fallback queries
It is permitted by line 20, because DNS replies ride inside HTTPS
It is denied by the implicit deny, because it is UDP and matches neither TCP permit line
q: Exhibit: Line 10: permit tcp any eq 80 any; Line 20: permit tcp any eq 443 any. The ACL is applied inbound on the WAN interface to allow return traffic for internal web users. Users report that web pages load but DNS name lookups time out. A DNS reply arrives from an external resolver, UDP source port 53, destined to a client's ephemeral port. What happens to that reply?

explain: Only an extended ACL can combine source, destination, protocol, and port in one decision. A standard ACL can judge source alone, so it would block either too much or too little no matter where it sits.
options: A standard ACL naming the user group's subnet, placed next to the server
An extended ACL matching source subnet, destination server, and TCP port 443
A standard ACL on the VTY lines of the application server
A standard ACL naming the server, placed next to the user group
q: A policy must block one user group from reaching a specific application server only on HTTPS, while the same group keeps access to that server's other services and to all other servers. Which ACL approach can express this rule?

explain: The range keyword covers every port from 8000 through 8100, so 8080 matches line 10 and is permitted immediately. Line 20 only catches this subnet's TCP traffic to the server on ports outside the permitted range.
options: It is permitted by line 10, because 8080 falls inside the 8000-8100 range
It is denied by line 20, because range entries are evaluated after plain deny entries
It is permitted by line 30, because 8080 is not an exact match for either earlier line
It is denied by the implicit deny, because range cannot be used with a host destination
q: Exhibit: Line 10: permit tcp 10.8.0.0 0.0.255.255 host 10.6.6.6 range 8000 8100; Line 20: deny tcp 10.8.0.0 0.0.255.255 host 10.6.6.6; Line 30: permit ip any any. A packet from 10.8.3.44 to 10.6.6.6 on TCP port 8080 arrives where the ACL is applied inbound. What happens?

explain: The established keyword matches TCP packets with the ACK or RST bit set, i.e. packets belonging to an existing session, so a bare SYN does not match line 10 and no other line covers it. Line 20 is a permit for UDP DNS, not a deny.
options: It is permitted by line 20, because new connections fall back to UDP checks
It is permitted by line 10, because established matches any TCP packet
It is denied by line 20 acting as a catch-all deny for TCP
It is denied by the implicit deny, because a lone SYN has neither the ACK nor RST flag that established requires
q: Exhibit: Line 10: permit tcp any any established; Line 20: permit udp any any eq 53. The ACL is applied inbound on the WAN interface. A TCP packet arrives from the internet with only the SYN flag set, starting a brand-new connection to an internal server. What happens?

explain: First match wins: the host deny on line 10 fires and the packet never reaches the subnet permit on line 20. Reversing the two lines would have permitted the host, which is why entry order matters as much as content.
options: It is denied by line 10, because the host deny is matched before line 20 is reached
It is permitted by line 20, because the /24 permit is evaluated before host entries
It is denied by the implicit deny, because line 10 and line 20 conflict and both are ignored
It is permitted, because a standard ACL cannot deny a host that its own subnet permits
q: Exhibit: Line 10: deny ip host 192.168.1.10 any; Line 20: permit ip 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 any. This standard ACL is applied inbound on the LAN interface. A packet from 192.168.1.10 to an internet address arrives. What happens?

explain: Because a standard ACL sees only the source address, applying it at the source drops that host's traffic to all destinations. The fix is to move a standard ACL close to the destination, or use an extended ACL that can name the file server and service.
options: Standard ACLs always block return traffic because they lack the established keyword
The implicit deny was removed, so the router failed closed on all other traffic
A standard ACL matches source only, so placed at the source it blocks that host from every destination, not just the file server
The ACL was numbered instead of named, so it defaulted to denying all protocols
q: To stop a single workstation from reaching one file server, an engineer applies a standard ACL permitting the design goal on the workstation's own access router, filtering inbound from the user LAN. Users then report the workstation cannot reach email, printers, or anything else either. What went wrong?

explain: An interface supports one ACL per protocol per direction, so separate inbound and outbound IPv4 ACLs are normal, and VTY access is restricted with access-class. A second inbound IPv4 ACL does not merge; the access-group command replaces rather than adds.
options: The access-class command can apply a standard ACL to restrict which sources may reach the VTY lines
An interface can have one IPv4 ACL applied inbound and a different IPv4 ACL applied outbound
VTY filtering is done with the ip access-group command under the interface facing the administrator
Two IPv4 ACLs applied inbound on the same interface are merged and both are fully processed
q: Which two statements about applying IPv4 ACLs are correct? (Choose two.)

explain: Evaluation follows sequence number order, not creation time, so line 5 denies the packet before line 10 can permit it. This is exactly why inserting a low sequence number is the standard way to change an ACL's behavior without rebuilding it.
options: It is permitted by line 20, because conflicting entries are skipped as a pair
It is denied by the implicit deny, because duplicate entries disable the ACL
It is denied, because the inserted line 5 is evaluated before the older permit on line 10
It is permitted, because line 10 was created first in time and keeps priority
q: Exhibit, after an edit inserted a new first entry: Line 5: deny tcp host 172.16.7.7 host 10.1.1.1 eq 443; Line 10: permit tcp host 172.16.7.7 host 10.1.1.1 eq 443; Line 20: permit ip any any. A packet from 172.16.7.7 to 10.1.1.1 on TCP port 443 arrives where the ACL is applied. What happens now?

explain: Wildcard 0.0.255.255 means the first two octets must be exactly 172.16, so 172.17.5.6 misses line 10, and it also misses line 20's 10.0.0.0 entry, so it falls to the implicit deny. The /12 private-range idea is tempting but the ACL checks the literal address and wildcard, not address-class summaries.
options: It is permitted, because the wildcard makes the second octet a don't-care
It is permitted, because private 172.16.0.0/12 addresses are all covered by that entry
It is denied by line 10 itself, which IOS converts to a deny for non-matching sources
It is denied by the implicit deny, because 172.17.5.6 does not match the 172.16.0.0/16 range the wildcard defines
q: Exhibit: Line 10: permit ip 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255 any; Line 20: permit ip 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 any. The ACL is applied inbound. A packet with source 172.17.5.6 arrives. What happens?

explain: In an extended ACL, an eq placed after the source address qualifies the source port, and clients originate from ephemeral ports, not 443. The port operator must sit after the destination address to match the server's HTTPS port.
options: The entry matches destination port 443 anyway, because eq is position-independent
The entry matches packets whose source port is 443, but clients send from ephemeral source ports, so their packets do not match and fall to the implicit deny
HTTPS fails because the ACL omitted the established keyword for the request packets
The entry is invalid and IOS silently treats eq 443 as a comment
q: An administrator meant to filter web traffic leaving the user subnet and configured 'permit tcp 10.3.0.0 0.0.255.255 eq 443 any', placing eq 443 immediately after the source subnet. Users with normal ephemeral source ports cannot reach HTTPS sites through this ACL. Why?

explain: A line's match counter increments when a packet actually matches that entry, and first-match processing means the packets never matched line 10 before reaching line 20. Counters increment for permits as well as denies, so they show which rule fired, not just drops.
options: The test packets did not match line 10 and were matched and processed by line 20
Line 20 is the last line, so all counters roll up into it regardless of matches
Line 10 is broken and must be reseeded with a lower sequence number
The test packets were dropped, because only denied packets increment counters
q: While testing an ACL change, an engineer sends five test packets and then checks 'show access-lists'. The match counter for line 20 has increased by five, while the counter for line 10 is unchanged. What does this prove?

explain: With DHCP snooping, ports are untrusted by default, and the port toward the real DHCP server (usually the uplink) must be configured with 'ip dhcp snooping trust'. Leaving it untrusted would cause legitimate offers from the server to be dropped.
options: All ports are trusted only for DHCP requests; server replies need no trust setting
All ports are untrusted; the uplink toward the legitimate DHCP server must be configured trusted
Ports are untrusted only if they also run port security; the DHCP server port needs no setting
All ports are trusted; the access ports facing PCs must be set untrusted manually
q: On a new access switch, DHCP snooping is planned for the user VLAN. By default, after snooping is enabled, how are the switch ports treated, and which port must be explicitly trusted?

explain: DHCP snooping is switched on globally with 'ip dhcp snooping' and then activated per VLAN with 'ip dhcp snooping vlan 20'. Trust is a separate per-interface setting, and ARP inspection is a different feature that depends on snooping.
options: 'ip dhcp snooping' followed by 'ip dhcp snooping vlan 20'
'switchport dhcp snooping vlan 20' in interface mode on the uplink
'ip arp inspection vlan 20' followed by 'ip dhcp snooping trust' globally
'ip dhcp snooping vlan 20' on every access interface only
q: A switch must run DHCP snooping only for VLAN 20. Which pair of global commands enables it for just that VLAN?

explain: Untrusted ports may send client messages such as Discover and Request, but server messages like Offer and Ack arriving on an untrusted port are dropped. That is the core rogue-server protection snooping provides.
options: It drops them, because DHCP server messages are not allowed to arrive on untrusted ports
It rate-limits them to one per minute so legitimate offers usually win
It forwards them but removes the rogue server's default gateway option
It forwards them only to clients that appear in the binding table
q: A rogue DHCP server is plugged into an untrusted access port on a snooping-enabled switch and starts sending DHCP Offer and Ack messages to clients. What does DHCP snooping do with those messages?

explain: The binding table ties a client's MAC address to its leased IP address on a specific VLAN and interface, built by watching DHCP transactions. It holds no credentials or hostname data, and dynamic ARP inspection later validates ARP packets against exactly these bindings.
options: The client's username, RADIUS realm, VLAN, and switch port
The client's public IP address, NAT translation, and ARP cache aging time
The client's MAC address, leased IP address, VLAN, and interface, learned from its DHCP exchange
The client's hostname, operating system, default gateway, and DNS servers
q: A help desk analyst asks what information the DHCP snooping binding table records for each client, since another security feature depends on it. Which set is correct?

explain: DAI validates ARP packets on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table, and a spoofed IP-to-MAC pairing fails that check and is dropped. This is what blunts ARP spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks; BPDU guard addresses a different threat entirely.
options: The ARP replies are forwarded, because ARP cannot be filtered by a Layer 2 switch
The ARP replies are dropped and the event is logged, because the IP-to-MAC pairing does not match the binding table
The switch shuts the port for BPDU guard violation

XML
explain: YAML represents structure with indentation and key-colon-value lines without braces or tags. JSON requires braces and quoted keys, and XML requires tags, so neither matches the description.

q: A team must choose a human-readable format for a REST API response that uses braces, quoted keys, and arrays, and is widely parsed by web applications. Which format best fits?
options: XML, because it is the only format REST can use
JSON, because it uses key-value pairs with braces and arrays
YAML, because REST responses require indentation only
Plain text with no structure
explain: JSON matches the braces, quoted keys, and arrays described and is common for REST APIs. RESTCONF can also use XML, so XML is not the only option, and YAML indentation alone does not match the described structure.

q: A team wants a configuration tool that installs no agent on managed nodes, connects over SSH, and uses YAML playbooks. Which tool meets all three requirements?
options: Ansible
Chef
Puppet
DNA Center assurance
explain: Ansible is agentless, uses SSH, and uses YAML playbooks. Puppet and Chef are both agent-based, so either one fails the agentless requirement even though they are configuration tools.

q: Managed servers run a dedicated agent that periodically checks in with a central master server, and configuration is written in manifests. Which tool is described?
options: Ansible
RESTCONF
Puppet
Chef
explain: Puppet uses an agent-based master/agent model with manifests. Ansible is agentless with playbooks, Chef uses cookbooks and recipes, and RESTCONF is an API protocol, not a configuration tool.

q: A configuration team organizes its code into cookbooks containing recipes written in a Ruby-based DSL, and managed nodes run an agent. Which tool is in use?
options: NETCONF
Ansible
Chef
Puppet
explain: Cookbooks, recipes, and a Ruby-based DSL with an agent describe Chef. Ansible uses YAML playbooks without an agent, Puppet uses manifests, and NETCONF is a protocol.

q: An engineer runs a YAML file that lists a set of tasks to configure NTP on a group of servers, without installing any software agent on those servers first. Which tool and artifact are being used?
options: Chef and a cookbook
Ansible and a playbook
DNA Center and an assurance dashboard
Puppet and a manifest
explain: A YAML file of tasks run agentlessly is an Ansible playbook. Chef uses cookbooks, Puppet uses manifests, and both of those tools are agent-based, unlike the scenario described.

q: Servers in a data center each run an agent. The agent contacts a master, obtains the desired state described in manifests, and enforces it. An engineer must name the tool for documentation. Which tool is it?
options: Ansible, because manifests are YAML playbooks
Ansible, because it is agent-based
Puppet, because the master/agent model with manifests is its model
Chef, because manifests are Ruby recipes
explain: The master/agent model with manifests identifies Puppet. Ansible is agentless and uses playbooks, and Chef uses cookbooks and recipes rather than manifests, so the other options mix up tool properties.

q: A device supports a protocol that carries configuration encoded in XML over an SSH connection and uses YANG models. Which protocol is this?
options: Northbound REST with basic auth only
SNMP polling over UDP only
RESTCONF
NETCONF
explain: NETCONF uses XML over SSH with YANG data models. RESTCONF is the HTTP-based counterpart that can use JSON or XML, so it does not match the SSH transport in the stem.

q: An application needs to manage a device over HTTP using REST principles, with data encoded in JSON and modeled by YANG. Which protocol best fits?
options: Puppet over SSH with manifests
Southbound forwarding in the data plane
NETCONF over SSH with XML only
RESTCONF over HTTP
explain: RESTCONF provides a REST-like HTTP interface to YANG-modeled data with JSON or XML encoding. NETCONF uses SSH rather than HTTP, so it fails the transport requirement.

q: A vendor document describes YANG as the language used to define the structure of configuration and operational data for network devices. Which statement about YANG is correct?
options: YANG is an HTTP status code set
YANG is an agent-based configuration tool
YANG is a data modeling language
YANG is a transport protocol that replaces SSH
explain: YANG is a data modeling language used by NETCONF and RESTCONF. The protocols provide transport, while configuration tools and status codes are separate concepts.

q: A NOC uses streaming telemetry and automation to flag degrading interface error rates and suggest likely causes before a link fails. At CCNA v1.1 awareness depth, how is this best described?
options: AI and ML replace all human network engineers
The data plane forwards packets using YANG
Automation with telemetry assists network assurance by helping detect and diagnose issues
Prompt engineering is used to configure switches
explain: At awareness depth, AI/ML-assisted assurance uses telemetry to help detect anomalies and likely causes. It assists engineers rather than replacing them, and it is unrelated to packet forwarding or prompt-based configuration.

q: An inventory API returns this data as flowing text: {"hostname": "CORE-SW2", "serial": "FOC2145A1", "software": "17.9"}. What is the hostname value in the response? (Choose the exact value.)
options: software
FOC2145A1
CORE-SW2
explain: The hostname key is paired with CORE-SW2. The serial value and software version are tempting alternatives, but they are values of different keys.

q: A controller API returns this data as flowing text: {"ap_name": "AP-Lobby-1", "status": "joined", "clients": 23}. How many clients are reported for the access point?
options: AP-Lobby-1
joined
explain: The clients key has the numeric value 23. The name and status values describe identity and state, not the client count.

q: Which two benefits are directly associated with replacing manual per-device changes with automation? (Choose two.)
options: Guaranteed elimination of all network outages
Faster deployment of changes at scale
Removal of the need for a data plane
More consistent configurations across devices
explain: Automation improves consistency by applying the same change everywhere and increases speed at scale. It does not guarantee zero outages, and the data plane is still required to forward traffic.

q: Which two statements describe a controller-based network compared with a traditional network? (Choose two.)
options: The controller provides a central management point for many devices
Policy is defined centrally on the controller
There is no management plane in a controller-based network
Each device must be configured separately by CLI for every policy change
explain: Controller-based networking centralizes policy definition and management for many devices. Separate per-device CLI for every change describes the traditional model, and a management plane still exists in the controller model.

q: Which two statements about SDN planes are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The control plane makes decisions about how traffic should be forwarded
The data plane forwards traffic based on forwarding information
The control plane forwards individual user packets out physical interfaces
The data plane calculates routing protocols centrally in the controller
explain: The control plane decides forwarding behavior and the data plane forwards traffic accordingly. Assigning routing calculation to the data plane or packet forwarding to the control plane reverses their roles.

q: Which two CRUD-to-HTTP mappings are correct? (Choose two.)
options: POST maps to create
PUT maps to read
GET maps to delete
DELETE maps to delete
explain: POST creates and DELETE deletes in the standard CRUD mapping. GET maps to read, not delete, and PUT maps to update, not read.

q: Which two functions are associated with Cisco DNA Center? (Choose two.)
options: Network assurance with device and client health information
Acting as an agent-based tool that uses Ruby cookbooks
Device discovery and inventory of network devices
Forwarding packets in the data plane of each switch
explain: DNA Center discovers and inventories devices and provides assurance and health visibility. Ruby cookbooks describe Chef, and DNA Center itself does not forward packets in a switch data plane.

q: Which two features are characteristic of JSON? (Choose two.)
options: Structure is defined only by indentation with no braces
Structure requires angle-bracket opening and closing tags
Data is organized as key-value pairs
Data can be organized in arrays using square brackets
explain: JSON uses key-value pairs and arrays in square brackets. Angle-bracket tags describe XML, and indentation-only structure describes YAML.

q: Which two statements are true of Ansible only, with no property borrowed from another tool? (Choose two.)
options: It organizes configuration into Ruby-based cookbooks
It is agentless on managed nodes
It requires an agent that checks in with a master
It uses YAML playbooks
explain: Ansible is agentless and uses YAML playbooks. The master-and-agent check-in describes Puppet, and Ruby-based cookbooks describe Chef.

q: Which two statements correctly distinguish NETCONF and RESTCONF? (Choose two.)
options: RESTCONF is a data modeling language
NETCONF is an agent-based configuration tool using manifests
NETCONF uses XML over SSH
RESTCONF uses HTTP and can carry JSON or XML
explain: NETCONF runs over SSH with XML, and RESTCONF runs over HTTP with JSON or XML, both using YANG models. Manifests belong to Puppet, and YANG, not RESTCONF, is the modeling language.

q: In a traditional network, an OSPF change requires an engineer to open separate management sessions to 15 routers. Which plane is the engineer interacting with on each router?
options: The data plane by forwarding user packets
The device-level management plane of each router
The northbound API of an SDN controller
The controller-level management plane only
explain: Separate sessions to each router are device-level management. There is no controller in this traditional scenario, and configuring OSPF is not data plane forwarding.

q: An SDN controller provides a single dashboard where an operator changes policy for an entire site at once. Which management characteristic does this show?
options: Device-level management with no central view
Manual management with no automation
Controller-level management with a centralized view
Data plane management by end hosts
explain: A single point that manages the whole site shows controller-level management with a centralized view. Device-level management would require handling each device separately.

q: During a change window, an automated job deploys the same QoS policy to 80 branches and logs identical successful results, while a previous manual rollout produced five variants. Which automation benefit is most evident from the identical results?
options: Replacement of HTTP with SSH
Elimination of the need for IP addressing
Creation of a new overlay protocol
Consistency of the applied configuration
explain: Identical successful results across branches demonstrate consistency. The scenario gives no evidence of a new overlay, addressing change, or protocol replacement.

q: A junior engineer manually entering a static route types the wrong next-hop address on one of ten routers, causing an outage for one branch. Which risk of traditional manual management does this illustrate?
options: Southbound API version mismatch
Controller failure affecting all devices at once
Human error from repetitive manual entry
YAML indentation failure in a playbook
explain: A typing mistake during repetitive manual entry is human error, a key risk automation reduces. No controller, southbound API, or playbook is involved in the scenario.

q: A service portal sends a request to an SDN controller asking it to reserve bandwidth for a video application, without directly configuring any switch. Which interface is the portal using?
options: The data plane interface of a router
The northbound interface of the controller
The console port of an access switch
The southbound interface to the switches
explain: Applications and portals communicate with the controller through its northbound interface. Southbound interfaces face the network devices, which the portal deliberately does not contact directly.

q: An SDN controller must push a new forwarding entry to a leaf switch and read its interface counters for verification. Which interface does the controller use for both actions?
options: The northbound interface toward a help desk portal
A YAML playbook with no protocol
The southbound interface toward network devices
The northbound interface toward applications
explain: Programming devices and reading device state are southbound functions between controller and devices. Northbound interfaces serve applications above the controller, not the switches below it.

q: A fabric design document lists leaf and spine switches, their loopback addresses, and the routing that lets every leaf reach every other leaf. Which layer of the design is documented?
options: The underlay
The intent layer
The northbound API
The overlay
explain: Physical switches and the IP routing providing reachability between them form the underlay. The overlay would be the virtual tunnel networks built on top of that reachability.

q: A tenant virtual network stops working. Troubleshooting shows the tunnels are configured correctly, but leaf switches cannot reach each other's loopback addresses. In which layer is the fault most likely located?
options: The data format layer, because JSON is not being used
The northbound API, because applications cannot reserve bandwidth
The underlay, because tunnel endpoints have lost IP reachability
The overlay, because tunnels are configured correctly
explain: Overlays depend on underlay reachability between tunnel endpoints, so loss of loopback reachability points to the underlay. Correctly configured tunnels cannot work without that underlying connectivity.

q: An architect states in DNA Center that contractors should reach only a specific application and never the finance servers. DNA Center generates and pushes the required policies to the fabric devices. Which two concepts are combined in this workflow?
options: Manual CLI entry and per-device management
Data plane forwarding and basic authentication
Agent-based management with manifests
Intent-based networking through a controller-based platform
explain: A stated business intent translated and pushed centrally by DNA Center combines intent-based networking with controller-based management. Manual CLI, packet forwarding, and Puppet manifests are not part of the workflow described.

q: A developer creates a new network object with a POST and the API replies with a body containing the new object ID and a success status for creation. Which status code most precisely confirms that a new resource was created?
explain: Status 201 specifically confirms resource creation after a POST. Status 200 is a tempting general success code, but it does not specifically signal that a new resource was created.

q: An assurance tool polls an API for a switch that was removed from inventory last week, and the API responds that the requested resource cannot be located. Which status code best matches the response described?
explain: A resource that cannot be located returns 404 Not Found. Status 403 would mean the authenticated caller lacked permission, and 500 would mean a server fault, neither of which is described.

q: An API call is sent with no token and no username or password, and the server replies that authentication is required before the request can be processed. Which status code should be documented for this failure?
explain: Status 401 indicates the request lacks valid authentication. Status 403 is tempting but applies after authentication when the user is not authorized for the action.

q: A read-only operations account successfully logs in to an API but receives an error when it tries to delete a device, because deletion requires an admin role. Which status code best fits?
options: 404, because the device does not exist
401, because the account failed to authenticate
400, because the request syntax was invalid
403, because the account authenticated but is not authorized for deletion
explain: The account authenticated successfully but lacks permission, which is 403 Forbidden. Status 401 would require an authentication failure, which contradicts the successful login in the stem.

q: A device API returns this data as flowing text: {"device": {"hostname": "DIST-SW1", "location": {"building": "B", "floor": 3}}}. On which floor is the device located according to the data?
options: Building B
Floor 3
The data contains no location information
DIST-SW1
explain: Inside the nested location object, the floor key has the value 3. Building B is the building value and DIST-SW1 is the hostname, so they do not answer the floor question.

q: A health API returns this data as flowing text: {"hostname": "R2", "interfaces": ["GigabitEthernet0/0", "GigabitEthernet0/1", "GigabitEthernet0/2"]}. How many interfaces are listed in the array?
options: 0, because names are not counted as elements
explain: The interfaces array contains three string elements, one for each listed interface. Each quoted name counts as an array element, so the count is three, not zero.

q: A trainee studies this data as flowing text: {"vlan_id": 20, "name": "VOICE"}. Which component is the key in the first key-value pair?
options: vlan_id
name
VOICE
explain: In the first pair, vlan_id is the key and 20 is its value. Name is the key of the second pair, and VOICE is that pair's value.

q: An engineer opens a text file that begins with a list of hosts, followed by indented tasks using name and module fields, with structure shown by spacing rather than braces. The file will be run to configure servers without agents. What is the file most likely to be?
options: A YAML playbook for Ansible
A Ruby cookbook for Chef
An XML document for NETCONF
A JSON response from a REST API
explain: Hosts plus indented tasks in YAML run agentlessly identify an Ansible playbook. XML and JSON have different syntax, and a Chef cookbook is Ruby-based and agent-based, which conflicts with the scenario.

q: A payload contains this content as flowing text: <interface><name>GigabitEthernet0/1</name><enabled>true</enabled></interface>. Which data format is used?
options: XML, because it uses opening and closing tags
JSON, because true is a boolean value
JSON, because it contains a key named enabled
YAML, because it uses indentation only
explain: Opening and closing angle-bracket tags identify XML regardless of the field names inside. JSON would use braces and quoted keys, and YAML would use indentation without tags.

q: Managed nodes each run an agent that periodically initiates contact with a central server to obtain and apply configuration organized as cookbooks. Which tool is in use?
options: Puppet
Ansible
Chef
DNA Center
explain: An agent model with cookbooks identifies Chef. Ansible is agentless, Puppet uses manifests rather than cookbooks, and DNA Center is a network platform, not this server configuration tool.

q: A comparison table must list one property per tool with no mixing. Which row is entirely correct for the tool named?
options: Chef: agent-based, uses cookbooks and recipes, uses a Ruby-based DSL
Puppet: agentless, uses YAML playbooks, connects by SSH with no agent
Chef: agentless, uses YAML playbooks, requires no agent
Ansible: agent-based, uses manifests, requires an agent on each node
explain: Chef is agent-based and uses cookbooks and recipes in a Ruby-based DSL, so that row is pure. The Ansible rows fail because Ansible is agentless with playbooks, and the Puppet row fails because Puppet is agent-based with manifests.

q: A team needs to configure Linux servers. Option 1 requires no agent and runs YAML playbooks over SSH. Option 2 uses cookbooks applied by an agent. Which pairing names the tools correctly?
options: Both options describe Ansible
Option 1 is Chef and Option 2 is Ansible
Both options describe Puppet
Option 1 is Ansible and Option 2 is Chef
explain: Agentless YAML playbooks over SSH describe Ansible, and agent-applied cookbooks describe Chef. Reversing the names is the tempting error, and Puppet uses manifests in neither description.

q: Two devices from different vendors both expose the same YANG model for interface configuration, allowing one automation workflow to manage both. Which benefit of model-driven programmability does this show?
options: YANG eliminates the need for any transport protocol
Data models forward packets in the data plane
Using a model removes the need for authentication
Vendor-neutral data models provide a consistent structure across devices
explain: A shared YANG model gives a consistent, vendor-neutral structure for the same data. A transport such as NETCONF or RESTCONF and authentication are still required, and models do not forward packets.

q: A junior engineer wants to test REST API calls against Cisco device models without risking production equipment, using Cisco-provided learning resources and sandboxes. Which program is this associated with?
options: Puppet master certification
HTTP status code registry
Cisco DevNet
Cisco DNA Center assurance only
explain: Cisco DevNet provides developer learning resources and sandboxes for practicing programmability safely. DNA Center assurance, Puppet, and status codes do not provide that sandbox learning environment.

q: Telemetry from many access points shows a pattern of roaming failures at one location, and an assurance system correlates the data and points engineers to a likely misconfiguration. Which statement best characterizes this capability at awareness depth?
options: Analytics over collected telemetry can assist engineers in detecting patterns and likely causes
The access points have stopped using a control plane
The system works by sending basic authentication to clients
Machine learning guarantees the fault will never recur
explain: Analytics and ML assist assurance by finding patterns in telemetry and suggesting likely causes. They do not guarantee faults will never recur, and the scenario involves neither plane changes nor client authentication.

q: A VLAN API returns this data as flowing text: {"vlan_id": 30, "name": "GUEST", "status": "active"}. What is the name assigned to VLAN 30 in the response?
options: vlan_id
active
GUEST
explain: The name key is paired with GUEST for VLAN 30. Active is the status value, and 30 is the VLAN ID itself, not its name.

q: A port API returns this data as flowing text: {"port": "GigabitEthernet1/0/5", "admin_status": "down", "oper_status": "down"}. What is the administrative status of the port?
options: down
GigabitEthernet1/0/5
oper_status
up
explain: The admin_status key has the value down. The port name identifies the interface, and oper_status is a separate key even though it happens to hold the same value here.

q: A discovery API returns this data as flowing text: {"device": "SW-CORE", "neighbors": ["R1", "SW-ACCESS1", "SW-ACCESS2"]}. Which devices are listed as neighbors of SW-CORE?
options: No neighbors, because neighbors is a key
R1, SW-ACCESS1, and SW-ACCESS2
SW-CORE, R1, and SW-ACCESS1 only
Only R1
explain: The neighbors array lists R1, SW-ACCESS1, and SW-ACCESS2. SW-CORE is the device itself, given by the device key, not a member of its own neighbors array.

q: A client receives HTTP 400 together with this body as flowing text: {"error": "invalid_input", "field": "vlan_id", "message": "vlan_id is required"}. Which field must the client correct to fix the request?
options: invalid_input
message
vlan_id
error
explain: The field key identifies vlan_id as the field at fault, and the message confirms it is required. Invalid_input is the error value, not the field name the client must supply.

q: An existing user object in a controller must have only its email address changed through a REST API, leaving the rest of the object unchanged. Which method is most appropriate for this partial update?
options: DELETE
POST
GET
PATCH
explain: PATCH applies a partial update to an existing resource. GET reads, POST creates, and DELETE removes, so none of them perform the partial change described.

q: A dashboard repeatedly polls an API with GET requests to display interface utilization. An engineer states that these polls should not modify device configuration. Why is this expectation correct?
options: GET is a read operation in the CRUD mapping
GET creates a backup before every change
GET requires an agent on the device
GET always returns status 201
explain: GET maps to read, so polling with GET retrieves data without modifying the resource. Creation returns 201 and uses POST, and GET has no agent requirement.

q: A company grows from 10 to 120 branch routers. Manual configuration time grows with every new router, and leadership asks for a scalable approach. Which recommendation best addresses the scaling problem?
options: Hire engineers to type faster on each CLI
Configure each router with a different manual procedure
Automate configuration with templates applied consistently to all routers
Remove the management plane from all routers
explain: Templates applied by automation scale to many routers while keeping configurations consistent. Faster typing and different manual procedures still scale poorly and increase variation and error.

q: An operator changes a security policy once in a controller, and within minutes all 60 managed switches enforce the new policy without individual logins. Which controller-based advantage is demonstrated?
options: Manual verification on every device CLI
Agent-based enforcement using cookbooks
Centralized policy change propagated to many devices
Data plane forwarding without a control plane
explain: Defining a policy once and having it propagated to all devices is the centralized advantage of controller-based networking. No per-device login, cookbook, or forwarding-plane change is described.

q: Unlike a traditional network where each device holds a partial view, an SDN controller maintains a view of the whole network topology. Which advantage does this central view most directly provide?
options: Each switch must still calculate every path independently
The data plane no longer needs forwarding tables
Decisions can be made with awareness of the entire network state
Applications no longer need any API to reach the controller
explain: A central topology view lets the controller make decisions using the whole network state. Devices still need forwarding entries, and applications still use northbound APIs to reach the controller.

q: Which two statements correctly distinguish the three data formats? (Choose two.)
options: JSON structure is defined only by indentation with no quoted keys
JSON uses key-value pairs enclosed in braces with quoted keys
YAML uses angle-bracket tags to enclose elements
XML uses opening and closing tags to enclose elements
explain: JSON uses braces with quoted keys in key-value pairs, and XML uses opening and closing tags. Angle-bracket tags belong to XML, not YAML, and indentation-only structure belongs to YAML, not JSON.

q: Which two statements describe how automation and telemetry assist network operations at CCNA v1.1 awareness depth? (Choose two.)
options: AI guarantees that human engineers are no longer needed for any decision
Telemetry replaces the data plane and forwards user traffic itself
Automation can apply corrective or configuration actions consistently across devices
Collected telemetry can be analyzed to highlight unhealthy devices or clients
explain: Telemetry analysis supports assurance by highlighting health issues, and automation applies actions consistently. Neither replaces engineers entirely nor takes over packet forwarding.
